## Tutorials

### End-to-end Payment Flow
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/tutorials/end-to-end-payment-flow

> Send a payment from wallet setup through settlement and reconciliation.

Follow one payment through its lifecycle:

1. **Create or pick the source wallet.** Create a custody wallet with [Set Up Wallets](/docs/guides/setup-wallets), or find one with `GET /v1/wallets`. Note its `id` (`cwlt_…`).
2. **Build the transfer.** Collect the destination address, token and amount, and check them before you send. See [Basic payment](/docs/payments/send-basic-payment).
3. **Send it.** Call `POST /v1/payments/transfers` with a new `Idempotency-Key`. SDP builds the transaction, has the source wallet's custody provider sign it, and submits it.
4. **Keep the identifiers.** Store the transfer `id` (`xfr_…`) and its `signature` with your own record.
5. **Wait for finality.** A successful request answers `finalized`. If it answers `processing`, read `GET /v1/payments/transfers/{transferId}` until it settles. See [Verifying a payment](/docs/payments/accept-verification).
6. **Reconcile.** Match the transfer to your ledger and update what your users see. See [Indexing and reconciliation](/docs/payments/accept-indexing).

The [Payments API reference](/docs/reference/api/payments) and [Wallets API reference](/docs/reference/api/wallets) have each endpoint's request and response.

---

## Developing with SDP

### Idempotency
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/developing-with-sdp/idempotency

> Retry mutations safely with Idempotency-Key, especially when moving money.

Clients time out, connections drop and workers die mid-run. Send an `Idempotency-Key` header so a retry returns the first attempt's answer instead of doing the work twice.

```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/transfers \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sf_..." \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: 0192f8a4-6c1e-7d4b-8f3a-b7e52c8d9f0a" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ ... }'
```

## Where keys apply

**Required.** These routes move money. A request without a key returns `400 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REQUIRED`, and nothing runs.

- `POST /v1/payments/transfers`
- `POST /v1/payments/transfer-batches`
- `POST /v1/payments/transfer-batches/{batchId}/retry`
- `POST /v1/payments/recurring-payments`
- `PATCH /v1/payments/recurring-payments/{id}` (an edit to an active schedule signs and broadcasts a replacement subscription)
- `POST /v1/payments/recurring-payments/{id}/activate`
- `POST /v1/payments/recurring-payments/{id}/cancel`
- `POST /v1/payments/recurring-payments/{id}/collect`
- `POST /v1/payments/recurring-payments/{id}/resume`

**Accepted.** The key is optional, and honored when sent.

- Wallets: `POST /v1/wallets`, `POST /v1/wallets/initialize`, `POST /v1/wallets/signer-check`, `PATCH /v1/wallets/{walletId}`, `DELETE /v1/wallets`
- Counterparties: `POST`, `PATCH` and `DELETE` on `/v1/counterparties` and on counterparty accounts
- Payment requests: `POST /v1/payments/requests` and `POST /v1/payments/requests/{paymentRequestId}/cancel`

**Not used.** `POST /v1/payments/transfer-batches/estimate` moves and stores nothing, so it does not read the key.

Modules with their own key handling say so on their pages, and each operation's API reference page lists the `Idempotency-Key` header when the route takes one.

## Choosing a key

- A key is 1–255 printable ASCII characters. Anything else returns `400`.
- Generate one key per logical operation (a UUIDv4 or UUIDv7 works well), store it with the operation before you send it, and send the same key on every retry of that operation.
- A new operation needs a new key, even when its request is identical to an earlier one.
- Keys are scoped to your organization, project, HTTP method and route, and bound to the credential that sent them. The same key value on two different routes is two separate keys.

A money request, saved with its key before the first send and retried under that key:

```typescript title="send-transfer.ts"
// Save the key with the operation first, so a restarted worker retries under it.
const payout = await db.payouts.create({ ...input, idempotencyKey: crypto.randomUUID() });

async function sendTransfer(payout: Payout): Promise<Response> {
  for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= 8; attempt++) {
    let response: Response;
    try {
      response = await fetch("https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/transfers", {
        method: "POST",
        headers: {
          Authorization: "Bearer sf_...",
          "Content-Type": "application/json",
          "Idempotency-Key": payout.idempotencyKey,
        },
        body: JSON.stringify(payout.request),
      });
    } catch {
      // The connection dropped: the transfer may have run, so retry under the same key.
      await backoff(attempt);
      continue;
    }
    if (!(await isRetryable(response))) return response;
    await backoff(attempt, response.headers.get("Retry-After"));
  }
  throw new Error(`Transfer ${payout.id} is still unanswered: retry later with the same key`);
}

async function isRetryable(response: Response): Promise<boolean> {
  // A money route answers a same-key retry after a 5xx from the record the first attempt wrote.
  if (response.status >= 500 || response.status === 429) return true;
  if (response.status !== 409) return false;
  const { error } = await response.clone().json();
  return error?.code === "IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_IN_FLIGHT";
}

function backoff(attempt: number, retryAfter?: string | null): Promise<void> {
  const ms = Math.max(Number(retryAfter ?? 0) * 1000, 250 * 2 ** attempt);
  return new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));
}
```

Every retry above sends the same body and the same key. Don't change the request to "fix" a retry: a different request under the key is `422 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED`.

## What a retry returns

Access is checked before the key on every request, so a retry passes exactly the checks a new request passes, and a request refused for access never claims the key.

| Situation | Response |
| --- | --- |
| Same key, same request, original finished | The original status and body, with the response header `Idempotent-Replayed: true`. |
| Same key, original still running | `409 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_IN_FLIGHT` with `Retry-After`. Wait, then retry with the same key. |
| Same key, original never recorded its outcome (it crashed) | Until 15 minutes plus the route's lease have passed since the original was sent (about 16 minutes, or about 20 for transfer batches), `409 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_IN_FLIGHT` with `Retry-After`, as if it were still running. After that, transfers, transfer batches, recurring payments and `POST /v1/wallets` take over and answer from the record the original wrote, and a payment request cancel runs again. A batch whose original stopped before sending some recipients answers with those recipients `failed`: they were never sent, so send them again with `POST /v1/payments/transfer-batches/{batchId}/retry`. Every other route returns `409 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_OUTCOME_UNKNOWN` with no `Retry-After`, to this and every later retry with the key: read the resource with `GET` to see whether it ran, then send again with a new key. |
| Same key, different request or different credential | `422 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED`. Nothing runs. |
| Same key, but the credential has since lost access to the wallet or resource | `403`. The stored response is not returned. |
| Original was refused with `400`, `401`, `403`, `409` or `429` before it wrote anything | Nothing was stored. Fix the cause and retry with the same key; the request runs again. |
| A transfer or transfer batch failed after writing its record (for example `400 TRANSACTION_FAILED`, or `409` for a signer mismatch) | Stored: the same error, with `Idempotent-Replayed: true`. After 24 hours the record answers with the same status and code. The key is spent: send the request again with a new key to try again. |
| A recipient is archived before recurring-payment activation | A fresh activation returns `404` before writing an attempt or signing. A completed activation still replays its saved response. Recovery can confirm saved transactions, but refuses to sign a new step for an unavailable recipient. |
| A recurring-payment action failed | An action refused before it sent anything leaves the schedule as it was, except that a collection with an unavailable counterparty or account pauses it with `pausedReason: "destination_unavailable"` and returns `409` without signing. If a cancel sent its transaction and confirming it then failed, SDP keeps the attempt and the schedule stays `canceling` until the attempt is recovered; poll `GET /v1/payments/recurring-payments/{id}`. A `400`, `401`, `403`, `409` or `429` (such as `TRANSACTION_FAILED`) is not stored, and a `5xx` is not replayed, so a same-key retry runs the action again. Any other `4xx`, such as `422 SIGNING_REJECTED` or `404`, is stored and replayed with `Idempotent-Replayed: true` for 24 hours; send a new key to try again sooner. |
| A recurring-payment action meets another key's unfinished attempt on the schedule | Cancel and collect return `409` (already processing), not stored; read the schedule with `GET`. An interrupted collect finishes on its own from the transaction SDP saved before sending it. Resume sends nothing on chain and commits in one step, so it is never left half-done. An interrupted activate or cancel is resumed in the background from the last step SDP recorded; SDP first reads each step it may already have sent from the chain, and a step is not sent again when the chain shows it landed. An interrupted `PATCH` resumes only when that `PATCH` is retried with its key (see below). A `PATCH` may finish that attempt and then applies its own change. |
| A keyed recurring-payment cancel, resume or `PATCH` changes nothing (such as canceling a canceled schedule) | It still records its attempt, so a same-key retry, even after 24 hours, is answered from it and never runs over a later change. |
| Original returned a `5xx` | Stored and replayed: use a new key to try again. The routes that move money are the exception: a same-key retry runs again and answers from the record the first attempt wrote, so it never sends twice. That answer also carries `Idempotent-Replayed: true`. A same-key retry of a payment request cancel also runs again. |

"Same request" means the same path, query parameters, body and credential. Recipient order in a transfer batch, and `"1.0"` versus `"1"` for an amount, do not change the request.

Keys are scoped to the credential that sent them. After API key rotation, the replacement key is a new credential: for 24 hours, a retry with the old `Idempotency-Key` gets `422`. Once the old record expires, that retry can run again and move money. A new `Idempotency-Key` can do the same. Before resending after rotation, read the resource with `GET` (for example, list transfers or read the recurring payment) to learn whether the original ran.

An organization that has been deleted or has lost production access is refused before the key is read: `401` or `403`, even for a retry of a request that completed.

## Replays are snapshots

A replay returns the response as it was first sent: a transfer stored as `processing` replays as `processing`. To see current state, read the resource with `GET`. Never re-send a request to learn its outcome.

An answer from the original record (a same-key retry after a `5xx` or the 24-hour window) reflects its current state. A recurring-payment lifecycle action may still be mid-transition; poll `GET /v1/payments/recurring-payments/{id}` until it settles.

An update left `updating` does not finish in the background. Retry its `PATCH` with the same key. Until the interrupted attempt is 15 minutes old, the retry gets `409 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_IN_FLIGHT` with `Retry-After`. After that, it resumes from the last recorded step without resending one the chain shows landed.

## Retention

Keys are kept for 24 hours after the original request. After that, a same-key retry on most accepted routes starts a new request. On the routes that move money, the record the first attempt wrote still holds its key, so a late retry is answered from that record, or refused if the request differs; a failed transfer answers with the status and code it failed with.

## Creating wallets

One `POST /v1/wallets` key maps to one recorded wallet. Same-key retries return it, even after 24 hours; a different request under that key returns `422`. A provider that accepts a request ID also receives one derived from the key, so it dedupes creation. A provider failure is stored as `503` for 24 hours. A new key is a new provider request.

An ambiguous `503` may mean the provider created a wallet before SDP received the result. Other providers do not dedupe on the request ID. If SDP wrote no wallet row, a same-key retry after 24 hours can create another wallet. Before retrying with any key, check `GET /v1/wallets` and, if needed, the provider account.

Provider request IDs and recorded-wallet lookups include the credential. After API key rotation and expiry of the 24-hour record, the old `Idempotency-Key` under the new API key becomes a new provider request and can create a second wallet. List wallets and check the provider account first.

## The dashboard and the Postman collection

The dashboard sends a key on every request to the routes that require one, and keeps it until it gets a definitive answer, so a retried click never moves money twice.

The [Postman collection](/docs/reference/postman-collection) saves one key per required operation in `idempotencyKey.<operationId>`. It creates the key only when the variable is empty and clears it only after a final-payment `2xx`, a replayed refusal, or a `422` other than `IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED`.

While a transfer, batch, or schedule remains `pending` or `processing`, Postman keeps the key. Poll with `GET` instead of resending, then clear the variable when final. It also keeps the key after timeouts, `5xx`, `409`, `429`, and `400`, `401`, or `403` refusals; the original request may still have run.

`422 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED` means the request differs from the original. Restore that request to retry. To start a new operation, first check with `GET` that the original settled, then clear the variable yourself.

## Recommendations

- Send a key on every mutation that accepts one, not only where it is required.
- Retry timeouts, connection errors and `409 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_IN_FLIGHT` with backoff, reusing the key.
- Treat `409 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_OUTCOME_UNKNOWN` as final for that key: check with `GET`, then use a new key.
- After a `5xx`, retry with the same key on the routes that move money; elsewhere, use a new key.
- Outside a key rotation, treat `422 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED` as a bug in your client: the key was attached to two different operations.
- Persist the returned resource ID before moving to the next operation, so a restarted worker can resume without guessing.

---

### Authentication
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/developing-with-sdp/authentication

> Authenticate requests with a project-scoped API key, limited by its grants, wallet scope, and IP allowlist.

Send your API key in the `Authorization` header. The example reads it from `SDP_API_KEY`:

```bash
curl 'https://api.solana.com/v1/wallets' \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SDP_API_KEY"
```

The `Bearer` prefix is optional; the header also accepts the bare key.

Each key carries three independent controls: grants, a wallet scope, and an IP allowlist. Together they give the key exactly the access its integration needs.

## Key scope

A key belongs to one **project** and inherits that project's environment: a key from a sandbox project reaches devnet, one from a production project mainnet-beta. The key itself doesn't name its environment; the dashboard shows it next to each key. A key reaches only its own project's resources. There is no cross-project or organization-wide key.

## Authorization layers

A request must clear every layer that is configured on its key:

| Layer | What it controls |
| --- | --- |
| **Grants** | The actions (`module.verb`) the key may perform. Each route needs exactly one; see [Grants by module](/docs/developing-with-sdp/manage-api-keys#grants-by-module) |
| **Wallet scope** | Which custody wallets SDP may sign with for the key: `all` in its project, or only the `selected` wallets in `walletIds`; see [Wallet access](/docs/developing-with-sdp/manage-api-keys#wallet-access) |
| **IP allowlist** | Optional IPv4 or IPv6 addresses and CIDR ranges the key may be used from. An organization-wide list under **Settings** > **API key access** applies to every key on top. Neither restricts signed-in dashboard members |

## Errors

Authentication and authorization failures are always machine-distinguishable: the code says what kind of refusal it is, and a `403` names what is missing in `error.details`.

| Condition | Status | Code | `error.details` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| No API key on a keyed-only request | 401 | `UNAUTHORIZED` | |
| Malformed or unknown key | 401 | `INVALID_API_KEY` | |
| Key has been revoked, its organization was deleted, or its project was archived | 401 | `REVOKED_API_KEY` | |
| Key is live but its organization is suspended; the key works again once SDP resumes it | 403 | `FORBIDDEN` | `reason: "organization_suspended"` |
| Key past its expiry or rotation deadline | 401 | `EXPIRED_API_KEY` | |
| Request origin not in the key's or the organization's IP allowlist | 403 | `FORBIDDEN` | `reason: "ip_not_allowed"` |
| Route only a signed-in dashboard member may use, such as managing keys, members or the organization | 403 | `FORBIDDEN` | `reason: "human_session_required"` |
| Key lacks the route's action, or the action a signature it asks for needs | 403 | `INSUFFICIENT_PERMISSIONS` | `action` names the missing action |
| SDP refused to sign for the request (see below) | 403 | `FORBIDDEN` | `reason` names why |
| Per-key rate limit exceeded | 429 | `RATE_LIMITED` | |

### Signing refusals

SDP decides again each time it signs on a key's behalf, so a change to the key or the organization applies to the next signature, including one later in the same request. Nothing is signed or sent on refusal. `error.details.reason` is one of:

| `reason` | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `wallet_out_of_scope` | The custody wallet is outside the key's wallet scope |
| `wallet_purpose` | The custody wallet's purpose may not send payments: only a `transfer` wallet can be the source of a transfer, transfer batch, or recurring payment |
| `principal_not_live` | The key was revoked, expired, or passed its rotation deadline during the request |
| `organization_inactive` | The organization is suspended or deleted |
| `production_not_enabled` | The project is a production project and the organization does not have production access |
| `project_not_found` | The project no longer exists |
| `principal_missing` | No credential is attached to the movement |
| `movement_disabled` | SDP has disabled this kind of money movement for the project |

A key without the action a signature needs is refused with `INSUFFICIENT_PERMISSIONS` and `error.details.action`, exactly as at the route.

Each key is rate limited by its tier. [Rate limits](/docs/reference/conventions/rate-limits) lists the limits.

See [Manage API Keys](/docs/developing-with-sdp/manage-api-keys) for creating, rotating, and revoking keys.

---

### Manage API Keys
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/developing-with-sdp/manage-api-keys

> Create, rotate, and revoke API keys with explicit grants by module, a signing wallet scope, and zero-downtime rotation.

API keys authenticate SDP API requests. Each key belongs to a project, inherits its environment, and holds an explicit list of grants plus optional controls. [Authentication](/docs/developing-with-sdp/authentication) covers how SDP enforces them.

Keys are credentials, not administrators. Only a signed-in organization admin creates, changes, rotates, or revokes a key, in the dashboard. An API key can't manage keys, the organization, its members, or project members, whatever it's granted: it's refused with `403 FORBIDDEN` and `error.details.reason` set to `human_session_required`.

SDP returns the full secret once, at creation and at rotation, and stores only a keyed hash of it. A lost key can't be recovered, only rotated or replaced. Every key records `lastUsedAt`, so you can find stale keys before you revoke them.

## Key format

Keys use the shared Solana Foundation format, `sf_<key id>_<secret><checksum>`:

| Part | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `<key id>` | 16 hex characters. Not secret: safe to log, and shown in the dashboard to tell keys apart |
| `<secret>` | 43 base62 characters (256 random bits) |
| `<checksum>` | 6 base62 characters, so a mistyped key is refused at once and secret scanners can match a leaked one |

The format doesn't name an environment: a key reaches the network of the project it was created in (sandbox: devnet, production: mainnet-beta). Keys created before this format, prefixed `sk_test_` or `sk_live_`, keep working until they are revoked.

## Grants by module

Every API route performs exactly one **action**, named `module.verb`, and a key may call a route only when it holds that action. A key holds an explicit list of grants: there is no role and no wildcard.

| Verb | What it allows |
| --- | --- |
| `read` | View the module's records |
| `manage` | Create and edit records reversibly: drafts, pausing, canceling |
| `execute` | Anything irreversible or that leaves SDP: onchain transactions, provider calls, moving money, and changing where money goes, such as a payout destination or a recurring amount |

`manage` and `execute` each include the same module's `read`. Nothing else implies another action: `execute` doesn't include `manage`, and a grant on one module gives nothing on another. Some modules add verbs of their own. These are the actions a key can be granted on this deployment:

| Module | Actions | Covers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `transfers` | `transfers.read`, `transfers.execute` | Single transfers from a custody wallet |
| `transfer_batches` | `transfer_batches.read`, `transfer_batches.execute` | Batches of transfers, and their estimates |
| `payment_requests` | `payment_requests.read`, `payment_requests.manage` | Payment requests and their payment links |
| `counterparties` | `counterparties.read`, `counterparties.manage`, `counterparties.execute` | Counterparties, their accounts, and provider requirements |
| `transactions` | `transactions.read` | The unified transaction list; each row also needs the read of its own module |
| `recurring` | `recurring.read`, `recurring.manage`, `recurring.execute` | Recurring payments and their collection attempts; on beta, also subscription plans and subscriptions |
| `wallets` | `wallets.read`, `wallets.manage`, `wallets.execute` | Custody wallets and their balances |
| `projects` | `projects.read` | Projects and provider availability |

Some actions are never granted to a key, because keys are credentials, not administrators: key, member, organization, and project administration, and every provider, credential, or connection setup (`configure`). A create or update naming one is refused with `400`. So is a grant on a module this deployment doesn't run; a key that already holds one keeps it when an update sends it back.

A request without the route's action is refused with `403 INSUFFICIENT_PERMISSIONS`, and `error.details.action` names the missing action. Nothing runs or is recorded on refusal. Grants are read on every request, so a change applies to the key's next request.

You can grant a key only actions you hold yourself. **Everything** in the dashboard writes out every action available when the key is created; an action added to SDP later isn't granted to existing keys.

## Wallet access

A key's wallet scope decides which custody wallets SDP may sign with on its behalf:

| `walletScope` | Signs with |
| --- | --- |
| `all` | Every custody wallet in the key's project |
| `selected` | Only the wallets listed in `walletIds`. With none listed, the key signs with no custody wallet; SDP's fee sponsor is outside wallet scope |

`walletIds` are custody wallet IDs, the `id` (`cwlt_…`) that `GET /v1/wallets` returns, not a provider's wallet ID. A key keeps the exact wallets you listed: a wallet created later, even one reusing a provider ID, is never added.

SDP checks the scope each time it signs, together with the key's grants and whether it's still active. A narrowed scope or a revoked key stops the next signature, including one later in the same request. A signature outside the scope is refused with `403 FORBIDDEN` and `error.details.reason` set to `wallet_out_of_scope`; nothing is signed or sent.

The scope narrows what a key may sign with, not what it may read. A `selected` key's wallet list (`GET /v1/wallets`) and wallet detail reads show only its wallets; every other read, such as transfers, batches, and recurring payments, covers the whole project. Give a separate project to an integration that must not see another's records.

For recurring payments the scope also bounds writes that sign nothing. A `selected` key may create, change, cancel, activate, collect, or resume only a recurring payment whose source wallet it lists, and may move one only to another listed wallet, because whoever activates a pending payment signs the terms it was last given. Anything else is refused with `wallet_out_of_scope` before it is recorded. Reading and listing recurring payments still cover the whole project.

The dashboard starts a key that holds any `execute` action on **Selected wallets**, so it can sign with nothing you didn't give it. Choose **All wallets** to widen it.

## Recurring payments outlive the key

A recurring payment is collected on schedule as its own mandate, not as the key or member that activated it. SDP checks that the payment is active, that it pays from its own source wallet, that its counterparty and account are active in the project, and that the organization may move money. Revoking or narrowing the key that activated it doesn't stop it, so rotating a key never interrupts a customer's schedule.

Archiving the counterparty archives its active accounts too, and new transfers and batches can't use them. Before the next new collection, an unavailable counterparty or account pauses the recurring payment with `pausedReason: "destination_unavailable"`. Work already in flight still recovers, and earlier requests still replay their recorded outcomes. The dashboard shows the pause reason and offers Cancel. Paused schedules can't be edited, so cancel the schedule and create a new one with an active recipient.

## Create a key

1. Open **API keys** in the sidebar. You start with an empty list.

   ![API keys page with no keys yet](/images/getting-started/api-keys-empty.png)

2. Click **Create new API key**. Once the project has keys, the button reads **New API key**. Fill in each step, then click **Continue**:
   - **Details**: a **Name** (for example, "CI deploy key"), an optional **Expiration**, and optional **Allowed IP addresses**, one IPv4 or IPv6 address or CIDR range per line. An empty list allows any address. The **Environment** is the project's.
   - **Permissions**: a checkbox per verb for each module (Read, Manage, Execute); ticking Manage or Execute includes Read. **Everything** ticks every offered action, and **Clear all** clears them. Grant at least one.
   - **Access**: **All wallets**, or **Selected wallets** with at least one wallet picked.

   ![Key details step of the new API key page](/images/getting-started/api-key-create.png)

3. On **Review API key**, check the summary and click **Create key**.

   ![Review API key step](/images/getting-started/api-key-review.png)

4. In the **API key generated** dialog, click **Copy** and save the key. It isn't shown again.

   <img src="/docs/images/getting-started/api-key-generated.png" alt="API key generated dialog with the full key redacted" width="512" height="313" style={{ display: "block", maxWidth: "100%", height: "auto" }} />

5. Click **Dismiss**. The key appears in the table with its prefix, permissions, wallet access, environment, and status.

   ![API keys list with one active key](/images/getting-started/api-keys-list.png)

To change a key's details, permissions, or wallets later, open its **Actions** menu and click **Edit API key**.

## Rotate a key

Rotation replaces the secret without downtime. The new key is a fresh record with the old key's grants, IP allowlist, wallet scope, and expiry. The old key keeps working until its grace deadline, 24 hours after a dashboard rotation; after that, it fails with `EXPIRED_API_KEY`.

1. In the API keys table, open the key's **Actions** menu, click **Rotate key (24h grace)**, then confirm with **Rotate key**.

   ![Actions menu with Edit API key, Rotate key (24h grace) and Delete key](/images/getting-started/api-key-rotate.png)

2. Copy the new key from the **API key generated** dialog. It's shown once.

## Revoke a key

Open the key's **Actions** menu and click **Delete key**. Type the key's name to confirm, then click **Delete key**. The key stops working on its next request and can't be restored. Deleting a rotated key during its grace period ends the overlap early: the replacement keeps working.

If the key may be compromised, tick **Also cancel recurring payments this key started** (`"cancelRecurringPayments": true` in the API). Otherwise its recurring payments keep collecting. The response lists canceled schedules and any you must cancel individually. A recurring payment answers to the key that activated or last resumed it, or last changed its source wallet, recipient, token, amount, or period. Metadata and next collection date changes don't change that control.

---

## Wallet operations

### Wallet balances
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/wallet-operations/balances

> Per-wallet token balances with optional USD valuation via SDP.

`GET /v1/payments/wallets/{walletId}/balances` returns a custody wallet's native **SOL** balance and every **SPL token** it holds, with raw and human-readable amounts, decimals, and a USD valuation where SDP has a price. SOL always comes first, as `token: "SOL"` with `mint: "So11111111111111111111111111111111111111112"`. Token accounts with a zero balance are left out.

## Request

`walletId` is the provider wallet ID: the `walletId` field from `GET /v1/wallets`, not the wallet's `id` (`cwlt_…`) or its address. The request needs an API key with `wallets.read`; a key limited to selected wallets reads only those.

<Tabs items={["curl", "TypeScript", "Java"]}>
<Tab value="curl">
```bash
curl 'https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/wallets/privy_wallet_123/balances' \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SDP_API_KEY"
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="TypeScript">
```typescript
const res = await fetch("https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/wallets/privy_wallet_123/balances", {
  method: "GET",
  headers: {
    Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.SDP_API_KEY}`
  }
});
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Java">
```java title="GetWalletBalances.java"
HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
    .uri(URI.create("https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/wallets/privy_wallet_123/balances"))
    .header("Authorization", "Bearer sf_...")
    .GET()
    .build();
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

If SDP can't read the SOL balance or any token balance, the request returns `503` instead of partial or zero balances. To read state no older than a slot you already saw, pass `minimumSlot`; the response echoes it in `data.balanceReadContext.minimumSlot`.

## Response shape

The payload sits in the standard `data` / `meta` envelope, with the balances in `data.walletBalances.balances`:

```json title="response.json"
{
  "data": {
    "walletBalances": {
      "walletId": "privy_wallet_123",
      "address": "3xYZa...2aBc",
      "balances": [
        {
          "token": "SOL",
          "mint": "So11111111111111111111111111111111111111112",
          "amount": "2500000000",
          "uiAmount": "2.5",
          "decimals": 9
        },
        {
          "token": "USDC",
          "mint": "EPjFWdd5AufqSSqeM2qN1xzybapC8G4wEGGkZwyTDt1v",
          "amount": "1500000000",
          "uiAmount": "1500",
          "decimals": 6,
          "usdPrice": 1,
          "usdValue": 1500
        }
      ]
    }
  },
  "meta": { "requestId": "req_...", "timestamp": "2026-05-18T00:00:00.000Z" }
}
```

Per-balance fields:

| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `token` | Token symbol if known, otherwise the onchain mint. |
| `mint` | Onchain mint address. |
| `amount` | Raw amount in the smallest unit (a string, to preserve precision). |
| `uiAmount` | Human-readable decimal string: `amount / 10^decimals`. |
| `decimals` | The token's decimal count. |
| `usdPrice` | Per-token USD price; omitted when no price is available. |
| `usdValue` | Total USD value (`usdPrice * uiAmount`); omitted when no price is available. |
| `confidential` | Reserved for confidential transfer balances; absent for standard balances. |

## Use cases

- **Account dashboards:** show a custody wallet's contents to its operator.
- **Pre-transfer balance checks:** confirm a wallet holds enough of a token before you start a payout batch.
- **Treasury accounting:** take periodic snapshots into an internal ledger.

## Pricing freshness

SDP prices balances only on mainnet. In a sandbox project on devnet, `usdPrice` and `usdValue` are always absent.

`usdPrice` is a display estimate from Tokens.xyz. SDP caches each price for up to 60 seconds. Some source snapshots refresh hourly; SDP omits snapshots older than two hours or without a timestamp. The snapshot timestamp doesn't prove when its underlying price was observed.

Use an executable quote for a trade and an independently verified valuation for accounting. The onchain `amount` and `uiAmount` remain the balance values. When pricing is unavailable, `usdPrice` and `usdValue` are absent: the omission means "unknown," not "$0.00."

## Compared with onchain RPC

You can also list SPL token balances by calling `getTokenAccountsByOwner` on a Solana RPC node and decoding the token-account data. Use SDP's balances endpoint for:

- **Token resolution:** SDP resolves the mint to a symbol when it knows one; raw RPC returns mints only.
- **USD pricing:** RPC has no prices.
- **One fewer dependency:** no separate RPC integration when you already call SDP.

Go to RPC directly for:

- **State at an exact slot:** for an audit that needs the wallet as of one slot. SDP's `minimumSlot` sets only a lower bound.
- **Confidential transfer balances:** full extension support is RPC-side.
- **Latency-sensitive paths:** RPC is one hop closer to the cluster.

## Related

- [Payouts and disbursements](/docs/payments/send-payouts): check balances before running a batch.
- [Create a wallet](/docs/guides/setup-wallets): provision the wallets whose balances this endpoint reports.

## Payments

### How payments work on SDP
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/payments/concepts

> Custody wallets, tokens, amounts, fees and the transfer record behind every SDP payment.

An SDP payment moves tokens from one of your custody wallets to a Solana address, and SDP records it as a transfer. This page covers the pieces the rest of the section builds on.

## Custody wallets

Every payment leaves from a **custody wallet** in your organization, optionally scoped to a project. A custody provider holds the wallet's key, and SDP asks that provider to sign. Limit what an API key can do with a wallet through [grants](/docs/developing-with-sdp/manage-api-keys#grants-by-module) and [wallet access](/docs/developing-with-sdp/manage-api-keys#wallet-access).

Create wallets first: see [Set Up Wallets](/docs/guides/setup-wallets). A transfer request names its source by the wallet's SDP `id` (`cwlt_…`) in `sourceCustodyWalletId`. Responses return that id as `custodyWalletId` and keep the provider's own wallet id in `providerWalletId`. The **destination** is the recipient's Solana address.

## Tokens and amounts

Pass `token` as `SOL` for native SOL, a well-known symbol such as `USDC`, or an SPL mint address. Pass a custom token by its mint. SDP resolves a symbol to its mint on your project's cluster and stores the mint on the transfer. The `token` filter on `GET /v1/payments/transfers` takes the same forms, and a well-known token matches whether you filter by symbol or by mint.

Amounts are decimal strings in whole-token units: `"100.00"` is 100 tokens, whatever the mint's decimals. Every amount you send SDP takes this form, and SDP converts it to base units when it builds the transaction. Wallet balance responses return both forms: `amount` in base units and `uiAmount` as a decimal string.

## Transfer execution

`POST /v1/payments/transfers` runs the whole transfer on the server. SDP builds the transaction, has the source wallet's custody provider sign it, submits it to your project's cluster, and waits for the cluster to finalize it before it answers.

## Fees and sponsorship

SDP pays the network fee, and the rent for any new recipient token account, on each transfer it signs from a Privy wallet. Those wallets need only the tokens they send, with no SOL for fees. Sponsorship has limits: when the sponsor can't pay, SDP refuses the transfer rather than charge the source wallet. A provider that submits its own transfers pays their fees from its own account, and SDP does not sponsor them.

## The transfer data model

Every transfer SDP sends or records is a `Transfer`. The fields most flows use:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | The SDP transfer id (`xfr_…`). Use it in API paths. |
| `status` | `processing`, `confirmed`, `finalized` or `failed` for a wallet transfer. See [Verifying a payment](/docs/payments/accept-verification). |
| `direction` | `outbound` (you paid) or `inbound` (you were paid). |
| `source`, `destination` | Solana addresses. |
| `counterpartyId` | The counterparty (`cpty_…`) the transfer is tied to, such as a [transfer batch](/docs/payments/send-payouts#native-transfer-batches) recipient or a transfer sent with `counterpartyAccountId`. |
| `token`, `amount` | What moved and how much. `token` is a mint address (some older records hold a symbol); `amount` is a decimal string such as `"100.00"`. |
| `memo` | Your note, up to 256 characters. SDP stores it; it is not written on chain. See [Payment with memo](/docs/payments/send-payment-with-memo). |
| `signature` | The Solana transaction signature, once there is one. Unique across SDP transfers. |
| `slot`, `blockTime`, `confirmedAt` | The slot the transaction landed in, its block time, and when SDP saw it land. `blockTime` is often `null` on transfers SDP sends. |
| `fee` | The network fee in lamports, when known. |
| `error` | Why the transfer failed. |

An outbound transfer starts at `processing`, and a successful `POST` usually answers `finalized`. See [Verifying a payment](/docs/payments/accept-verification#status-lifecycle) for every status and what it means.

## What SDP does and does not give you

You get what you need to **send**, **track** and **reconcile** payments transfer by transfer: status reads, filtered lists, wallet balances, `Idempotency-Key` replay, and a unique `signature` per transfer (see [Basic payment](/docs/payments/send-basic-payment#deduplication)). The public API has no checkout session or invoice object. [Accept payments](/docs/payments/accept-overview) covers the dashboard's payment links and how to build checkout on transfers.

## Related

- [Payments API reference](/docs/reference/api/payments): every payments endpoint.
- [End-to-end payment flow](/docs/tutorials/end-to-end-payment-flow): the same lifecycle as a step-by-step tutorial.

## Payments — Send Payments

### Basic payment
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/payments/send-basic-payment

> Send one token transfer from a custody wallet to a Solana address, from the dashboard or the API.

A basic payment moves tokens from a custody wallet you control to a Solana wallet address. Send it from **Payments** in the dashboard or with `POST /v1/payments/transfers`.

Pass `sourceCustodyWalletId` as the wallet's SDP `id` (`cwlt_…` from `GET /v1/wallets`). Pass `destination` as the recipient's wallet (owner) address, **not** a token account: for an SPL token, SDP derives the recipient's associated token account and creates it if it is missing.

## Prerequisites

- A custody wallet that holds the tokens you want to send, with a custody signer configured so SDP can sign for it.
- In the dashboard: a role that can send payments, and a contact to pay. Add contacts under **Payments** > **Contacts**.
- With the API: a key holding the `transfers.execute` grant whose [wallet access](/docs/developing-with-sdp/manage-api-keys#wallet-access) includes the source wallet. SDP checks the grant at the route and the key's access to the wallet again when it signs.

## How it works

<HowItWorks>

<Step number={1} title="Set up the transfer">

Specify the source, destination, token, and amount.

<StepPanel>
<Tabs items={["UI", "API"]} groupId="how-it-works">
<Tab value="UI">

Go to **Payments** in the sidebar. The overview shows your **Available balance**, recent **Activity**, and the **Move money** actions.

![Payments overview with the available balance, the Move money actions and recent activity](/images/payments/payments-overview.png)

Click **Pay**. The **Single** tab opens on the **Details** step, "Who are you paying?". Fill in:

- **Contact**: the person or business you are paying.
- **Destination**: one of the contact's Solana addresses. Click **Add a Solana address** to add one here.
- **Source wallet**: the wallet the payment leaves from.
- **Amount**: in whole-token units, such as `0.5`, with the token picked beside it.
- **Memo** (optional): a note SDP stores with the transfer. It is not written on chain.

![Details step with the source wallet list open](/images/payments/pay-source-wallet.png)

![Details step with every field filled in](/images/payments/pay-details-filled.png)

</Tab>
<Tab value="API">

Build the request body:

```typescript title="transfer-request.ts"
const body = {
  sourceCustodyWalletId: "cwlt_123",    // `id` from GET /v1/wallets
  destination: "7xKXz...9fGh",         // recipient wallet (owner) address
  token: "9aBCd...4eEf",               // mint address, SOL, or a symbol such as USDC
  amount: "100.00",                    // whole-token units, as a string
  memo: "Payment for invoice #1234",
};
```

</StepPanel>

A successful request waits for finality and returns the transfer at `finalized`. A `processing` answer means it is still settling: don't send it again, read it instead (step 3).

## Pay a counterparty

When `destination` is a saved counterparty's Solana address, pass that account's id (`cpacct_…`) as `counterpartyAccountId`. SDP ties the transfer to the counterparty, as it does for a [transfer batch](/docs/payments/send-payouts#native-transfer-batches) recipient: the transfer carries `counterpartyId`, and `GET /v1/payments/transfers?counterpartyId=` lists it. The dashboard's Pay flow does this for you.

The account must be an active `crypto_wallet` account in the same project, and
`destination` must be its address. An unknown or inactive account returns `404`,
any other mismatch returns `400`, and no transfer is created.

Only fields documented for your deployment are accepted. Unknown fields return
`400` during validation, before looking up a wallet or transfer.

## SOL and the rent-exempt minimum

A Solana wallet holds either nothing or at least the rent-exempt minimum (about 0.00089 SOL). SDP refuses a native SOL transfer with `409 AMOUNT_BELOW_RENT_MINIMUM` if it would fund an empty address below that minimum or leave the source with a nonzero balance below it. Nothing is written or sent.

`details.recipientIndexes` (`[0]`) or `details.sourceRemainder` identifies the problem; `details.minimumAmount` gives the minimum. Fund the address, send at least the minimum, or send the source wallet's whole balance. The `409` is not stored under the `Idempotency-Key`, so the same request can run after the balance changes. Token transfers are unaffected: SDP sponsors rent for a missing token account.

## Insufficient funds

When the source wallet holds less SOL, or less of the token in its token account, than the amount, the transfer fails with `400 TRANSACTION_FAILED` and nothing is sent. The transfer is recorded `failed`, and its `error` says the wallet does not have enough funds. Fund the wallet, then send the payment again with a new `Idempotency-Key`: the failed key replays the same error.

A source wallet that has never held the token has no token account for it, so the request is refused earlier with `400 BAD_REQUEST` ("Source wallet has no token account for this mint").

## Deduplication

`POST /v1/payments/transfers` requires an `Idempotency-Key`; without one it returns `400 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REQUIRED`. Use one stable key per payment and reuse it for retries. A same-key retry returns the original transfer. A changed request, wallet, or credential returns `422 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED`; an in-flight request returns `409 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_IN_FLIGHT` with `Retry-After`.

A recorded failure (such as `400 TRANSACTION_FAILED`, or `422 CUSTODY_POLICY_REFUSED` when the wallet's policy at its custody provider refused to sign) replays the same error; use a new key to try again. Replays are snapshots, so read the transfer with `GET` for its current status. See [Idempotency](/docs/developing-with-sdp/idempotency) for the full contract.

Persist the returned `Transfer.id` as your local primary key. Once populated, the on-chain `signature` is also unique across SDP transfers and can deduplicate records across SDP and another chain indexer.

See [Payouts and disbursements](/docs/payments/send-payouts#dedup-and-retries-for-single-transfers) for the same pattern applied to a run of transfers.

## Related

- [Payment with memo](/docs/payments/send-payment-with-memo): carry an order reference in `memo`.
- [Payouts and disbursements](/docs/payments/send-payouts): pay many recipients in one batch.
- [Verifying a payment](/docs/payments/accept-verification): transfer statuses and finality.

### Payment with memo
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/payments/send-payment-with-memo

> Attach an order id, invoice number or customer reference to an SDP transfer with the memo field.

Set `memo` on `POST /v1/payments/transfers` to store a note of up to 256 characters with the transfer. SDP returns it whenever you read or list that transfer, so your reconciliation can map each transfer back to a row in your own database.

## When to use a memo

Use a memo for a correlation value your backend already has when it sends the payment:

- **Order or invoice ids**: `order_2026-05-14_4837`, so the transfer ties to a checkout row.
- **Customer references**: your customer or account id, for support and reconciliation.
- **Run ids**: one payout run's id across many outbound transfers.

SDP stores the memo on its own record. It does **not** add a Solana memo instruction to the transaction, so block explorers don't show it. See [Memos and Solana Pay references](#memos-and-solana-pay-references) for on-chain correlation.

## API usage

<Tabs items={["curl", "TypeScript", "Java"]}>
<Tab value="curl">
```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/transfers \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sf_..." \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: order-2026-05-14-4837" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "sourceCustodyWalletId": "cwlt_123",
    "destination": "7xKXz...9fGh",
    "token": "9aBCd...4eEf",
    "amount": "100.00",
    "memo": "order_2026-05-14_4837"
  }'
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="TypeScript">
```typescript title="send-payment-with-memo.ts"

      "Content-Type": "application/json",
    },
    body: JSON.stringify({
      sourceCustodyWalletId: "cwlt_123",
      destination: "7xKXz...9fGh",
      token: "9aBCd...4eEf",
      amount: "100.00",
      memo: "order_2026-05-14_4837",
    }),
  }
);
const { data } = await response.json();
```
</Tab>

```java title="SendPaymentWithMemo.java"
        {
          "sourceCustodyWalletId": "cwlt_123",
          "destination": "7xKXz...9fGh",

        }"""))

```
</Tab>

The memo comes back on the transfer:

```json title="response.json"
{
  "data": {
    "transfer": {
      "id": "xfr_...",
      "memo": "order_2026-05-14_4837",
      "status": "finalized",
      "signature": "5xR1...",
      ...
    }
  }
}
```

`memo` takes up to 256 characters of UTF-8 text. Sanitize it on the way in if your downstream systems are stricter.

## Memos and Solana Pay references

A **Solana Pay reference** is the other way to correlate a payment: a unique public key per order, added to the transfer instruction. Anyone can then find and verify the payment on chain without SDP's database, and the payer can build the transfer from a Solana Pay URL.

SDP uses references for dashboard [payment requests](/docs/payments/accept-overview#payment-requests): each request gets its own, and SDP watches it to see when the request is paid. A transfer you send through the API carries no reference, and transfer records don't expose one. To read a reference from any transaction, fetch it from Solana RPC by its `signature`.

Rule of thumb: use a memo when **you** send the transfer (payouts, internal moves), and a reference when **someone else** does (customer checkout, donations).

## Finding transfers by memo

`GET /v1/payments/transfers` and `GET /v1/payments/transfers/{transferId}` return `memo`. To find transfers by memo, pass `search` with 3 or more characters: it matches part of the memo, as well as ids, signatures, addresses and counterparty names. See [Indexing and reconciliation](/docs/payments/accept-indexing) for query patterns.

## Related

- [Basic payment](/docs/payments/send-basic-payment): the transfer endpoint.
- [Payouts and disbursements](/docs/payments/send-payouts): tag every transfer in a run with one memo.
- [Accept overview](/docs/payments/accept-overview): payment requests and references for inbound payments.

### Payouts and disbursements
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/payments/send-payouts

> Pay many recipients in one batch, retry without paying anyone twice, and reconcile a payout run with SDP.

A payout run pays many recipients at once: marketplace sellers, payroll, affiliates, royalties. Use `POST /v1/payments/transfer-batches` when every recipient is a saved counterparty account. To pay arbitrary Solana addresses, call `POST /v1/payments/transfers` once per recipient and reconcile the transfer ids it returns.

## Native transfer batches

One request creates a durable batch, chunks its recipients into Solana transactions, and returns the batch, recipient, and transfer records:

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/transfer-batches \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sf_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: 3f0c9e7a-5b1d-4c2e-9a8f-6d4b2e1c0a97" \
  -d '{
    "externalId": "payroll-2026-05",
    "sourceCustodyWalletId": "cwlt_123",
    "token": "9aBCd...4eEf",
    "recipients": [
      {
        "externalId": "row_4837",
        "counterpartyId": "cpty_4837",
        "counterpartyAccountId": "cpacct_4837",
        "amount": "150.00"
      }
    ]
  }'
```

Each recipient names a counterparty account (`cpacct_…`) that is an active `crypto_wallet` account in the project. `counterpartyId` is optional; if you pass it, it must be that account's counterparty. An unknown, archived or mismatched account returns `404`. A batch takes up to 500 recipients.

The two ids do different jobs:

- **`Idempotency-Key`** (required) identifies this one request. Reuse it to retry that exact request after a timeout; recipient order does not change the request. Any unique value works, such as a UUID.
- **`externalId`** (required: a batch without one returns `400`) identifies the payout run. Derive it from your own data, such as the pay period, so every attempt at the run carries the same value. See [One batch per payout run](#one-batch-per-payout-run).

Use `GET /v1/payments/transfer-batches/{batchId}` to inspect recipient and chunk outcomes.

### One batch per payout run

The batch `externalId` names the payout run, and it is unique per project and source wallet. Whatever `Idempotency-Key` it carries, a batch with an `externalId` already used on that wallet never pays anyone again:

- The same request, from the same API key, returns the existing batch as it stands. A worker that restarts with a fresh key gets the original run back.
- Any other request (different recipients, amounts or options, or another API key) returns `409 TRANSFER_BATCH_RUN_EXISTS` with the existing batch in `error.details.batchId`. A replay only goes to the API key that sent the run, so after a key rotation the new key gets the 409: read the batch by its id instead of resending.

Derive the `externalId` from data you already have, so a worker that crashes and restarts computes the same value without storing anything: `payroll-2026-05`, `invoice-run-8812`. Never generate it at random: a random value is new on every attempt and protects nothing. New recipients go in a new run with a new `externalId`, never in a renamed copy of a run that was already sent.

```ts title="payroll-worker.ts"
// Safe to run again after a crash: the run's id comes from the period, not from storage.
const externalId = `payroll-${period}`;
const response = await fetch("https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/transfer-batches", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.SDP_API_KEY}`,
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
    "Idempotency-Key": crypto.randomUUID(),
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({ externalId, sourceCustodyWalletId, token, recipients }),
});
const body = await response.json();
// 200: this run's batch, new or replayed. 409 TRANSFER_BATCH_RUN_EXISTS: the run was
// already sent with a different body; read error.details.batchId instead of resending.
// A 5xx may come after the run was sent: its outcome is unknown, so run again with the
// same externalId, which returns the batch if it exists. A 4xx (a 409
// AMOUNT_BELOW_RENT_MINIMUM, say) is refused before anything is sent: report it.
let batchId: string;
if (response.ok) {
  batchId = body.data.batch.id;
} else if (body.error.code === "TRANSFER_BATCH_RUN_EXISTS") {
  batchId = body.error.details.batchId;
} else if (response.status >= 500) {
  throw new Error(`Payout run ${externalId} has an unknown outcome: run it again`);
} else {
  throw new Error(`Payout run ${externalId} was refused: ${body.error.code}`);
}
```

### Recovering from a partial failure

A batch with `failed` recipients paid some recipients and not others. A `failed` recipient was not paid: its transaction never reached the network, or the network rejected it. Its `error` says why; when the source wallet could not cover the amount, it reads "The wallet used for this payment does not have enough funds", so fund the wallet before you retry. To finish the run, retry the batch:

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/transfer-batches/{batchId}/retry \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sf_..." \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: 8b2e4f1c-7d3a-4e9b-a6c5-1f0d9e8c7b6a"
```

The retry sends only the batch's `failed` recipients, to the addresses the batch recorded for them, from the same wallet with the batch's options, and returns the batch with those recipients `processing` again. Recipients still `pending` or `processing` may still land, so they are never sent again. Each resent recipient keeps its row in the batch and links to its new transfer.

- Use a new `Idempotency-Key` for each retry you mean to send. The same key never sends again, including after a timeout or a server error, so resend a lost answer under the same key. It returns the saved response while that is stored, which can still show recipients `processing`: read the batch with `GET /v1/payments/transfer-batches/{batchId}` for its current state. If recipients fail again later, a retry under that old key sends nothing.
- Any API key that may send from the batch's wallet can retry it, not only the one that created it.
- A batch with nothing `failed` returns `409 TRANSFER_BATCH_NOTHING_TO_RETRY`, and a retry that loses to a concurrent one returns `409 TRANSFER_BATCH_RETRY_CLAIMED`. Nothing is sent. While a batch is `processing`, a recipient its request never sent becomes `failed` only once that request can no longer send it, so retry after the batch settles.
- A failed recipient whose counterparty account changed its address since the batch was sent is not paid either address: the retry returns `409 TRANSFER_BATCH_DESTINATION_CHANGED` naming it in `error.details.recipientIds`, and nothing is sent. Send that recipient in a new batch.
- A native SOL recipient paid less than the rent-exempt minimum at an address with no account fails again for the same reason, so the retry is refused with `409 AMOUNT_BELOW_RENT_MINIMUM` and that recipient stays `failed`. Send it in a new batch with a larger amount.
- Only recipients that are still `failed` are ever sent, so a retry under a new key never pays anyone twice.

Never resend the whole batch under a new `Idempotency-Key` to finish it: that pays the recipients who already succeeded again.

### The SOL rent-exempt minimum

A Solana wallet holds either nothing or at least the rent-exempt minimum (about 0.00089 SOL), and the network refuses a native SOL transfer that would break that, along with every recipient in the same transaction. SDP checks before it sends:

- A recipient whose address has no account must receive at least the minimum.
- The source wallet must end with nothing or at least the minimum. Chunks land in any order, so a batch that sends the wallet's whole balance also needs every chunk to move at least the minimum.

`POST /v1/payments/transfer-batches/estimate` lists what would fail in `estimate.warnings` (`AMOUNT_BELOW_RENT_MINIMUM` per recipient, `SOURCE_BELOW_RENT_MINIMUM` for the source). `POST /v1/payments/transfer-batches` refuses the batch with `409 AMOUNT_BELOW_RENT_MINIMUM`, naming `details.recipientIndexes` and `details.sourceRemainder`, before anything is written or sent. The 409 is not stored under the `Idempotency-Key`, so the same request runs again once it would clear. Token batches are unaffected: SDP funds a missing token account's rent (`tokenAccountRentLamports`).

### Token account rent per transaction

SDP funds new recipient token accounts up to a per-transaction rent limit. A chunk includes only as many new accounts as that limit covers; existing accounts are packed by count and size. The estimate's `transactionCount` is the number of transactions create submits. If one account exceeds the limit, create is refused with `409 SPONSORED_RENT_OVER_CAP` (`details.recipientIndex`) before anything is written or sent. Create that token account first.

## Paying recipients one transfer at a time

To pay destinations that are not saved counterparty accounts, send one transfer per recipient instead of a batch:

1. **Resolve recipients** in your application: the rows to pay, each with a destination address and an amount.
2. **Pick a run id** you control, such as `payout_2026-05-14_marketplace_sellers`.
3. **Send** each recipient a `POST /v1/payments/transfers` with the destination, amount, token, and a memo that holds the run id and the row (`payout_2026-05-14_marketplace_sellers/row_4837`).
4. **Store** the returned transfer `id` and `status` with the recipient row, so you can read the status again later.
5. **Reconcile** once every row is sent: list `GET /v1/payments/transfers?direction=outbound&from=…&to=…` and check that every row has a matching `finalized` transfer.

Send transfers sequentially or in modest concurrency (4–8 in flight); high concurrency increases the chance of priority-fee contention and blockhash expiry without much throughput gain.

To tie a single transfer to a saved counterparty account, pass `counterpartyAccountId` with it. See [Pay a counterparty](/docs/payments/send-basic-payment#pay-a-counterparty).

### Dedup and retries for single transfers

Two layers keep a worker that dies mid-run from paying anyone twice:

1. **Idempotency keys**: `POST /v1/payments/transfers` requires an `Idempotency-Key`. Give each recipient row one stable key and reuse it for retries. A retry with the same key and request returns the original transfer. Reusing the key for a different request returns `422 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED`, and a retry while the original is still running returns `409 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_IN_FLIGHT`.
2. **Application mapping**: store each row's transfer `id` before you move to the next row. On restart, retry with the row's same key, or skip rows that already have a transfer `id`.

A new key is a new payment, even with an identical body. The `signature` is unique across SDP transfers once set: use it to cross-check another indexer, not to retry.

<Tabs items={["curl", "TypeScript", "Java"]}>
<Tab value="curl">
```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/transfers \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sf_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: payout-row-4837" \
  -d '{
    "sourceCustodyWalletId": "cwlt_123",
    "destination": "7xKXz...9fGh",
    "token": "9aBCd...4eEf",
    "amount": "150.00",
    "memo": "payout_2026-05-14_marketplace_sellers/row_4837"
  }'
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="TypeScript">
```typescript title="payout-recipient.ts"
async function payoutRecipient(row: PayoutRow): Promise<string> {
  if (row.transferId) return row.transferId; // already submitted

  const response = await fetch(
    "https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/transfers",
    {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        "Authorization": "Bearer sf_...",
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": row.idempotencyKey,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify({
        sourceCustodyWalletId: row.sourceCustodyWalletId,
        destination: row.destination,
        token: row.token,
        amount: row.amount,
        memo: `${row.batchId}/row_${row.id}`,
      }),
    }
  );

  const { data } = await response.json();
  // The transfer record is under data.transfer (standard SDP success envelope).
  await row.persistTransferId(data.transfer.id); // persist BEFORE returning
  return data.transfer.id;
}
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Java">
```java title="PayoutRecipient.java"
HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
    .uri(URI.create("https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/transfers"))
    .header("Authorization", "Bearer sf_...")
    .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
    .header("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)
    .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString("""
        {
          "sourceCustodyWalletId": "%s",
          "destination": "%s",
          "token": "%s",
          "amount": "%s",
          "memo": "%s/row_%s"
        }""".formatted(sourceCustodyWalletId, destination, token, amount, batchId, rowId)))
    .build();
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

## Reconciling a run

After the loop finishes, list all outbound transfers in the run's time window and tally against your recipient table:

<Tabs items={["curl", "TypeScript"]}>
<Tab value="curl">
```bash title="Terminal"
curl "https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/transfers?direction=outbound&from=2026-05-14T00:00:00Z&to=2026-05-14T23:59:59Z&pageSize=100" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sf_..."
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="TypeScript">
```typescript title="list-outbound-transfers.ts"
async function* listOutboundTransfers(from: string, to: string) {
  let page = 1;
  while (true) {
    const url = new URL("https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/transfers");
    url.searchParams.set("direction", "outbound");
    url.searchParams.set("from", from);
    url.searchParams.set("to", to);
    url.searchParams.set("page", String(page));
    url.searchParams.set("pageSize", "100");

    const res = await fetch(url, {
      headers: { Authorization: "Bearer sf_..." },
    });
    const { data, meta } = await res.json();
    yield* data;
    if (!meta.hasMore) return;
    page += 1;
  }
}
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

To scope the list to one run, add `search=<run id>`, which matches part of the memo, or filter on `memo.startsWith(runId)` yourself. Match each recipient row by its transfer `id`.

## Failure modes

Handle these outcomes for each transfer:

- **`failed`**: the transfer never reached the network, or the network rejected it (insufficient funds, frozen account, expired blockhash). `error` says why. The recipient was not paid; to retry, send a new transfer with a new `Idempotency-Key`.
- **`processing` for longer than you expect**: the request stopped waiting before the chain settled the transfer. Read it with `GET /v1/payments/transfers/{transferId}` instead of sending it again, and send a new transfer only once `status` is `failed`.
- **Mid-run worker crash**: resume with each row's original `Idempotency-Key`, and store the returned transfer `id` before you move on.
- **Fee sponsor unavailable**: SDP pays the network fee on every transfer it signs, so the source wallet never needs SOL for fees. When the sponsor can't pay, SDP refuses the transfer without charging the source wallet.

## Related

- [Basic payment](/docs/payments/send-basic-payment): the transfer endpoint.
- [Payment with memo](/docs/payments/send-payment-with-memo): the memo field that tags a run.
- [Indexing and reconciliation](/docs/payments/accept-indexing): the same list endpoint, used for inbound payments.
- [Manage API keys](/docs/developing-with-sdp/manage-api-keys#grants-by-module): limit a payout key to the actions payouts need.

## Payments — Accept Payments

### Accept payments
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/payments/accept-overview

> Get paid into a wallet you control, through a dashboard payment link or a shared address, and find each payment.

To accept a payment, the payer sends tokens to one of your custody wallets and you find that payment. Send a payment link from the dashboard, or share a wallet address and detect payments yourself. [Verifying a payment](/docs/payments/accept-verification) covers when a payment is final, and [Indexing and reconciliation](/docs/payments/accept-indexing) covers listing and matching.

## Payment requests

In the dashboard, open **Payments** > **Requests**, click **New**, and set the amount, token, destination wallet and when the link expires. You get a link and a Solana Pay QR code that anyone can pay, and SDP pays the network fee for the payer's transaction. Each request gets its own Solana Pay reference, which SDP watches to see when the request is paid.

When a request is paid, SDP records an inbound `finalized` transfer with `kind: request_deposit`, which `GET /v1/payments/transfers?direction=inbound` returns. Create one in the dashboard or with `POST /v1/payments/requests`, and cancel it with `POST /v1/payments/requests/{paymentRequestId}/cancel`.

## Share a wallet address

Give the payer a custody wallet's Solana address. Copy it from **Payments** > **Deposit**, or read `publicKey` from [`GET /v1/wallets/{walletId}`](/docs/reference/api/wallets) (add `includeBalance=false` to skip the balance read). The payer sends an ordinary SOL or SPL transfer from any wallet. To offer a QR code, build a Solana Pay URL from the address, token mint and amount yourself.

SDP does not record these payments. You see them through `GET /v1/payments/transfers` with that wallet's `custodyWalletId` and `includeObserved=true`, which reads the wallet's recent on-chain history. These observed rows carry no memo or reference, and they never reach `finalized`; see [Observed transfers](/docs/payments/accept-indexing#observed-transfers).

### Match payments to orders

An observed payment's on-record keys are the wallet it landed in and its `destination`. To tell payments apart, give each order (or each customer) its own receiving wallet. One wallet per merchant, seller or ledger account works when you don't need to match single payments, such as treasury or settlement flows. To correlate by memo or Solana Pay reference instead, read the transaction from Solana RPC by its `signature`.

## What SDP gives you

- **Payment links**: payment requests, from the dashboard or `POST /v1/payments/requests`, recorded as inbound transfers once paid.
- **Observed payments**: a wallet's recent on-chain activity, from `GET /v1/payments/transfers?custodyWalletId=…&includeObserved=true`. See [Indexing and reconciliation](/docs/payments/accept-indexing).
- **Status reads**: `GET /v1/payments/transfers/{transferId}` for one recorded transfer. See [Verifying a payment](/docs/payments/accept-verification).
- **Balances**: `GET /v1/payments/wallets/{walletId}/balances`, where `walletId` is the provider wallet id (`walletId` from `GET /v1/wallets`). See [Wallet balances](/docs/wallet-operations/balances).

## What SDP does not give you

- **No checkout or payment-intent API**: a payment request is the only object you create ahead of a payment. Match payments to a shared wallet address against the order records you keep.
- **No settlement webhooks**: poll for status. See [Polling cadence](/docs/payments/accept-verification#polling-cadence).

## Example: a marketplace checkout

A minimal accept flow on per-order wallets:

1. At checkout, create a custody wallet for the order, or take one from a pool you keep. Store its `id`, its `publicKey`, the token and the expected amount on your `orders` row.
2. Show the payer the address, token and amount, or a Solana Pay QR code you build from them.
3. The payer's wallet sends the transfer.
4. Your worker polls each open order's wallet with `custodyWalletId` and `includeObserved=true`, and looks for an inbound transfer whose `token` and `amount` fit the order. Observed reads have their own quota, so space the polls out.
5. Check with Solana RPC that the transfer's `signature` is `finalized`, then mark the order paid. Store the `signature` so a rerun of the worker never applies the payment twice.

Treat your `orders` table as the checkout state machine and SDP as the wallet and settlement backend.

## Next steps

- [Verifying a payment](/docs/payments/accept-verification): statuses, and when a payment is safe to act on.
- [Indexing and reconciliation](/docs/payments/accept-indexing): list transfers, dedupe, and run a polling worker.

---

### Verifying a payment
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/payments/accept-verification

> Transfer statuses, finality on Solana, polling, and how to check a payment against the chain yourself.

A transfer's `status` tells you whether a payment landed and whether it can still be undone. This page covers each status, when a payment is safe to act on, and how to check it against the chain.

## Status lifecycle

A wallet transfer, sent or received, has one of these statuses:

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `processing` | Outbound and in flight: SDP is signing and submitting it, or waiting for the chain. `signature` can still be `null`. |
| `confirmed` | The transaction landed in a block that a supermajority of the cluster voted for. `signature` and `slot` are set. Not yet irreversible. |
| `finalized` | The block is finalized. Irreversible. |
| `failed` | The transfer never reached the network, or the network rejected it. The recipient was not paid; `error` says why. |

`POST /v1/payments/transfers` waits for finality, so a successful request usually answers `finalized`. If the wait runs out, it answers `processing`, and SDP moves the transfer to `confirmed`, `finalized` or `failed` as the chain settles. A `processing` transfer that never got a `signature` fails after 5 minutes, unless it is waiting on a custody approval.

Inbound payments differ. A paid payment request is recorded at `finalized`. An observed row (from `includeObserved=true`) shows `confirmed` or `failed` and never `finalized`, because SDP rebuilds it from chain history on each read. Check its finality yourself; see [Independent verification](#independent-verification).

`finalized` and `failed` are final. Transfers that other modules create document their own lifecycle.

## Finality on Solana

Act on `finalized` for anything irreversible: releasing custody, shipping high-value goods, posting to your general ledger. A `confirmed` transaction has a supermajority vote but can, rarely, still be dropped. Use it for low-stakes steps, such as a status email or a "paid" badge.

## Polling cadence

SDP sends no settlement webhooks, so poll:

- `GET /v1/payments/transfers/{transferId}` for one recorded transfer.
- `GET /v1/payments/transfers` for a time window or one wallet's activity. See [Indexing and reconciliation](/docs/payments/accept-indexing).

Start from these ranges:

- **Active checkout** (someone is watching the payment screen): every 2–5 seconds for up to a minute, then back off.
- **Background reconciliation** (no one is waiting): every 15–30 seconds, or on each worker tick.
- **After the fact**: one read when your application needs the answer, with no loop.

Every poll counts against your key's [rate limit](/docs/reference/conventions/rate-limits). Reads with `includeObserved=true` also count against their own quota of 30 a minute per API key, so spread them across your open orders.

## Independent verification

Once a transfer has a `signature`, you can check it against the network yourself:

- **`signature`**: open it on [Solana Explorer](https://explorer.solana.com/), or look it up with `getSignatureStatuses` on your own RPC.
- **`slot`**: the slot the transaction landed in.
- **`blockTime`**: the block's timestamp (ISO 8601). It is often `null` on transfers SDP sends; `confirmedAt` records when SDP saw the transaction land.
- **`fee`**: the network fee in lamports, when known.

If you run your own indexer, compare its view of each `signature` with SDP's `status`.

## Failure handling

When `status` is `failed`:

- Read `error` for the reason.
- Decide whether to try again. The failed transfer stays failed, and its `Idempotency-Key` replays the failure. To retry, send a new request with a new key; it creates a new transfer with its own `id` and `signature`.
- Tell whoever needs to know: the merchant, the customer, your operations team.

## Related

- [Accept overview](/docs/payments/accept-overview): payment requests and shared addresses.
- [Indexing and reconciliation](/docs/payments/accept-indexing): list and match many transfers.
- [Concepts: the transfer data model](/docs/payments/concepts#the-transfer-data-model): every transfer field.
