### Indexing and reconciliation
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/payments/accept-indexing

> List transfers, read a wallet's observed payments, dedupe, and reconcile against your own ledger.

`GET /v1/payments/transfers` lists the transfers SDP has recorded in your project, including what you sent (single, batch and recurring) and paid payment requests. Filter by direction, status, token, wallet, counterparty and date. To also see payments SDP never recorded, such as a customer's direct transfer to your address, pass one wallet's `custodyWalletId` with `includeObserved=true`.

## Listing inbound transfers

The minimal inbound request:

<Tabs items={["curl", "TypeScript"]}>
<Tab value="curl">
```bash title="Terminal"
curl "https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/transfers?direction=inbound&pageSize=50" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sf_..."
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="TypeScript">
```typescript title="list-inbound-transfers.ts"
const url = new URL("https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/transfers");
url.searchParams.set("direction", "inbound");
url.searchParams.set("pageSize", "50");

const res = await fetch(url, {
  headers: { Authorization: "Bearer sf_..." },
});
const { data, meta } = await res.json();
// data: Transfer[]
// meta: { total, page, pageSize, hasMore, requestId }
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

Without `includeObserved`, this returns recorded inbound transfers only, such as paid payment requests.

### Query parameters

| Parameter | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `direction` | `inbound` \| `outbound` | Inbound is a payment into one of your wallets. |
| `status` | string | One or more of `processing`, `confirmed`, `finalized`, `failed`, comma-separated. |
| `custodyWalletId` | string | One wallet's SDP `id` (`cwlt_…` from `GET /v1/wallets`). |
| `includeObserved` | boolean | Default `false`. With `custodyWalletId`, adds the wallet's recent on-chain activity; see [Observed transfers](#observed-transfers). |
| `token` | string | A well-known symbol (`SOL`, `USDC`) or a mint address. A well-known token matches either form. |
| `counterpartyId` | string | Transfers tied to one counterparty (`cpty_…`). |
| `search` | string | 3 or more characters, matched against ids, signatures, addresses, memo and counterparty names. |
| `from`, `to` | ISO 8601 datetime | Window on `createdAt`. Include a time zone, such as `2026-05-14T00:00:00Z`. |
| `sortBy`, `sortDirection` | string | Default `createdAt`, `desc`. |
| `page`, `pageSize` | integer | Default `1` and `20`. `pageSize` is at most `100`. |

[List transfers](/docs/reference/api/payments/list-payment-transfers) has every parameter.

## Observed transfers

With `custodyWalletId` and `includeObserved=true`, the list adds what the wallet's recent on-chain history shows and SDP has no record of:

- SDP builds these rows from the wallet's latest signatures (at most 200) on each read, and does not store them. Use them for recent activity, not history.
- Their `id` starts with `xfr_observed_`. It stays the same across reads, but `GET /v1/payments/transfers/{transferId}` does not find it.
- `status` is `confirmed` or `failed`, never `finalized`. `custodyWalletId` is `null`, and there is no `memo`.
- Reads with `includeObserved=true` have their own quota: 30 a minute per API key and 120 per organization. Past it they return `429 RATE_LIMITED`.

## Deduplication

- **Recorded transfers**: key them by `id` (`xfr_…`), which exists before any `signature` does. Once set, `signature` is unique across SDP's recorded transfers, so it also dedupes against another chain indexer.
- **Observed rows**: key them by `id`, not `signature`. One transaction can produce more than one row.

## Reconciling an order

For a customer's direct payment, the on-record keys are the receiving wallet and `destination`: observed rows carry no memo or reference. Give each order its own receiving wallet (see [Accept payments](/docs/payments/accept-overview#match-payments-to-orders)), then for each open order:

1. **Read** every page of the wallet's inbound activity, while `meta.hasMore` is `true`: `GET /v1/payments/transfers?custodyWalletId=<cwlt_…>&includeObserved=true&direction=inbound&pageSize=100`.
2. **Match** a transfer whose `token` and `amount` fit the order.
3. **Check finality**: observed rows stop at `confirmed`, so check with Solana RPC (`getSignatureStatuses`) that the `signature` is `finalized` before any irreversible step.
4. **Apply** the payment once: mark the order paid, store the `signature`, and start downstream work (email, shipment, ledger entry).
5. **Leave unmatched transfers** for the next pass, or flag them for review after a grace period.

A paid payment request needs none of this: SDP records it as an inbound `finalized` transfer.

## A polling worker

A worker that checks each open order's wallet on every tick:

<Tabs items={["TypeScript"]}>
<Tab value="TypeScript">
```typescript title="reconcile-tick.ts"
// Observed reads have their own quota (30 a minute per API key), and each
// page is one read. Past it, the worker waits out Retry-After and reads the
// same page again, so no order is skipped.
const sleep = (ms: number) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));

async function reconcileTick(openOrders: Order[]) {
  orders: for (const order of openOrders) {
    let page = 1;
    while (true) {
      const url = new URL("https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/transfers");
      url.searchParams.set("custodyWalletId", order.custodyWalletId);
      url.searchParams.set("includeObserved", "true");
      url.searchParams.set("direction", "inbound");
      url.searchParams.set("pageSize", "100");
      url.searchParams.set("page", String(page));

      const res = await fetch(url, {
        headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.SDP_API_KEY}` },
      });
      if (res.status === 429) {
        await sleep(Number(res.headers.get("Retry-After")) * 1000);
        continue; // the same page again
      }
      const { data, meta } = await res.json();

      for (const tr of data) {
        if (tr.status === "failed" || (await alreadyApplied(tr.id))) continue;
        if (tr.token !== order.mint || !sameAmount(tr.amount, order.amount)) continue;
        // Observed rows stop at "confirmed": check finality with your own RPC.
        if (!(await isFinalized(tr.signature))) continue;
        await markOrderPaid(order, tr); // stores tr.id and tr.signature
        continue orders; // paid: apply it once, then move to the next order
      }
      if (!meta.hasMore) break;
      page++;
    }
  }
}
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

Stop polling an order's wallet once the order is paid or expired, so the quota goes to open orders. `sameAmount` compares decimal strings by value: `"100"` and `"100.00"` are the same amount.

- [Accept overview](/docs/payments/accept-overview): payment requests and shared addresses.
- [Payouts and disbursements](/docs/payments/send-payouts): the same list endpoint, used for outbound runs.

## Self-Hosting

### Quickstart
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/self-hosting/quickstart

> Install the self-hosted stack, generate a .env, and bring it up with Docker Compose.

Go from an empty host to a running Solana Developer Platform. You need Docker Engine and Docker Compose v2, with the Docker daemon running.

## 1. Install

Run the install script. It downloads the latest release's `compose.yml` and `.env.example` into `~/sdp` and checks them against the release's `SHA256SUMS`. When `cosign` is installed, it also verifies the signature on `SHA256SUMS`.

```bash title="Terminal"
curl -fsSL https://github.com/solana-foundation/solana-developer-platform/releases/latest/download/install.sh | bash
```

The script is open source: read it before you run it. Its header shows how to verify the checksums and signature yourself, and lists the variables you can override, such as `SDP_INSTALL_DIR` and `INSTALL_VERSION` (a release tag to install instead of the latest).

To install by hand, download `compose.yml` and `default.env.example` from the [latest release](https://github.com/solana-foundation/solana-developer-platform/releases/latest) into a working directory, and save the second file as `.env.example`.

## 2. Generate your `.env`

The stack reads its configuration from a `.env` next to `compose.yml`. The [configurator](/docs/self-hosting/configurator) fills it in, generates the app secrets, and validates your answers.

- **In your browser:** open the [configurator](/docs/self-hosting/configurator), answer the prompts, and save the `.env` into `~/sdp`.
- **In your terminal:** run the configurator from the API image. Put the release tag you installed in place of `latest`, so the configurator matches your `compose.yml`. The install script prints this command with your tag filled in.

  ```bash title="Terminal"
  docker run --rm -it -v "$HOME/sdp:/out" \
    ghcr.io/solana-foundation/sdp/sdp-api:latest \
    node configure.js --out /out/.env
  ```

The [environment reference](/docs/self-hosting/env-reference) explains each variable.

## 3. Bring up the stack

```bash title="Terminal"
cd ~/sdp
docker compose up -d
```

`sdp-migrate` applies the database migrations first. The API starts next, and the dashboard and docs follow once it's healthy. The first run pulls the images, so it can take a few minutes.

## 4. Verify

```bash title="Terminal"
docker compose ps
docker compose logs -f sdp-api
```

Once the services report healthy, the dashboard is at `http://localhost:3000`, the API at `http://localhost:8787`, and these docs at `http://localhost:3001`. Point uptime checks at the API's [health endpoints](/docs/reference/api/health): `/health` says the API is up, and `/health/ready` also checks the database and Redis.

If a service fails to start or a required variable is missing, see [Troubleshooting](/docs/self-hosting/troubleshooting).

## Next steps

- [First devnet deployment](/docs/self-hosting/first-devnet-deployment): sign in to the dashboard, create a local wallet, and call the API.
- [Upgrade and backup](/docs/self-hosting/upgrade-and-backup): keep the stack current and protect your data.
- [Environment reference](/docs/self-hosting/env-reference): tune ports, RPC, signing, and authentication.

---

### First Devnet Deployment
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/self-hosting/first-devnet-deployment

> Run self-hosted SDP on devnet, sign in to the dashboard, create a local wallet, and verify API access.

Take a fresh self-hosted install from healthy containers to a first devnet workflow: dashboard sign-in, a local custody wallet, a wallet-scoped API key, and an authenticated API call.

Start after the [Quickstart](/docs/self-hosting/quickstart). This path runs on devnet with the local signer. Set up a provider's signing later, when you harden the deployment.

<Callout type="warn">
The public devnet RPC endpoint is fine for smoke tests, but it can rate-limit you or miss data that balance-heavy wallet views need. Use a dedicated devnet endpoint from your RPC provider before you rely on this flow.
</Callout>

<Steps>

<Step>

## Confirm the stack is healthy

From the directory that holds `compose.yml` and `.env`:

```bash title="Terminal"
cd ~/sdp
docker compose up -d
docker compose ps
curl http://localhost:8787/health
```

The health check returns JSON with `"status": "ok"`. The dashboard is at `http://localhost:3000`, the API at `http://localhost:8787`, and these docs at `http://localhost:3001`.

</Step>

<Step>

## Configure Clerk for dashboard sign-in

In your Clerk development application, follow the [Clerk setup guide](https://github.com/solana-foundation/solana-developer-platform/blob/main/apps/sdp-api/docs/self-hosting/clerk-setup.md):

- Turn on **Organizations**.
- Customize the session token (**Sessions** → **Customize session token**) with the guide's claims. Without `org_id`, the API refuses every dashboard request.
- Copy the publishable key, secret key, and issuer for the configurator.
- Give the API a public HTTPS URL, because Clerk can't reach `localhost`. To test locally, reserve a free static domain at [dashboard.ngrok.com/domains](https://dashboard.ngrok.com/domains) and run `ngrok http --url=<your-domain> 8787`.
- Add a webhook endpoint at `https://<your-domain>/webhooks/clerk/link-orgs`, subscribed to the events the guide lists. Copy its signing secret for `CLERK_WEBHOOK_SECRET`.

The API starts without `CLERK_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, but this tutorial needs it. The webhook is how SDP learns the settings you add to the organization in Clerk, including the one that turns on the local signer.

</Step>

<Step>

## Generate the devnet `.env`

Open the [configurator](/docs/self-hosting/configurator), keep its defaults, and fill in:

- `SOLANA_RPC_DEFAULT_DEVNET_API_KEY_URL`: your devnet RPC endpoint.
- The Clerk publishable key, secret key, issuer, and webhook secret.

The signing step keeps the local signer and generates its `CUSTODY_PRIVATE_KEY` in your browser. SDP offers the local signer only while that key is set. Save the file as `~/sdp/.env`, then restart the stack:

```bash title="Terminal"
cd ~/sdp
docker compose up -d
```

</Step>

<Step>

## Sign in to the dashboard

Open `http://localhost:3000`, sign in through Clerk, and create an organization when prompted. SDP creates it with you as its admin, along with a sandbox project and a production project.

If requests fail after sign-in, read the failing request's `401` response. `Clerk token missing organization` means the session token lacks the `org_id` claim, and `Clerk token has no usable email claim` means its `email` claim is wrong: fix the session token customization.

If Clerk's webhook deliveries fail, check the API logs:

```bash title="Terminal"
docker compose logs -f sdp-api
```

`webhooks: refused a Clerk webhook with an invalid signature` means `CLERK_WEBHOOK_SECRET` doesn't match the endpoint's signing secret. Clerk's delivery log shows the same refusal as `Invalid webhook signature`.

</Step>

<Step>

## Turn on the local signer

The local signer needs a per-organization activation. In the Clerk dashboard, open your organization's private metadata (**Organizations** → your organization → **Metadata** → **Private**) and add:

```json
{ "sdp": { "providerOverrides": { "custody": { "local": true } } } }
```

The `organization.updated` webhook brings it into SDP. Until it does, choosing the local signer returns `403` with `Local requires manual activation for this organization.`

</Step>

<Step>

## Create a local custody wallet

In the dashboard, open **Wallets**, choose the local provider, and create a wallet named `Devnet local wallet`.

This step needs the dashboard. Setting up a custody provider takes `wallets.configure`, which no API key can hold, so an organization admin does it signed in. After that, a key with `wallets.manage` can create more wallets with `POST /v1/wallets`.

</Step>

<Step>

## Create a wallet-scoped API key

Open **API keys** and create a key in the sandbox project. Under **Permissions**, grant at least `wallets.read`. Under **Access**, choose **Selected wallets** and select `Devnet local wallet`: it's the only wallet the key can sign with.

Copy the full key when the dashboard shows it. SDP shows it only once.

</Step>

<Step>

## Verify the key can read wallets

Call your self-hosted API with the new key:

```bash title="Terminal"
export SDP_API_KEY="sf_..."

curl "http://localhost:8787/v1/wallets?view=summary" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SDP_API_KEY"
```

The response includes `Devnet local wallet`. You now have a self-hosted devnet stack with dashboard sign-in, local custody signing, and an API key bound to the wallet it may sign with.

</Step>

</Steps>

- Use the [Environment reference](/docs/self-hosting/env-reference) to move from localhost defaults to real domains, an external Postgres, or an external Redis.
- Read [Upgrade and backup](/docs/self-hosting/upgrade-and-backup) before you keep data you care about in the stack.
- Use [External co-signers](/docs/self-hosting/external-co-signers) when a provider needs a signing process outside the default stack.

> Generate a complete .env for a self-hosted Solana Developer Platform, entirely in your browser.

Answer the steps below to generate a ready-to-use `.env` for the default devnet path. Everything runs in your browser, and nothing you enter is sent anywhere. Save the file next to `compose.yml`, then run `docker compose up -d`.

To continue after you download it, follow [First devnet deployment](/docs/self-hosting/first-devnet-deployment).

### Environment Reference
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/self-hosting/env-reference

> The configuration variables a self-hosted Solana Developer Platform reads from .env.

The stack reads one `.env` file next to `compose.yml`. The [configurator](/docs/self-hosting/configurator) writes it, with the defaults and validation of the release you installed. This page covers how the file is organized and the variables you're most likely to set by hand.

The configurator groups the variables into sections:

| Section | What it covers |
|---|---|
| Basic | `ENVIRONMENT`. The deployment mode is always `self_hosted`. |
| Database | Bundled Postgres or an external database. |
| Cache | Bundled Redis or an external one. |
| Solana RPC | The devnet and mainnet RPC endpoints. |
| Authentication (Clerk) | Clerk keys, issuer, dashboard URL, and webhook secret. |
| Signing provider | Which signers to enable, the default one, and their credentials. |
| Fee payment | The Kora that sponsors each cluster's transaction fees, if any. |
| Secrets | App secrets, generated where you run the configurator. |
| Advanced | Image source, ports, public URLs, proxy trust, and optional features. |

## Required variables

`compose.yml` refuses to start without these:

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` | Password for the bundled Postgres. Required even with an external `DATABASE_URL`, because the bundled `postgres` service still starts. |
| `API_KEY_PEPPER` | Server-side pepper for API key hashes. Generate it with `openssl rand -hex 32`. |
| `CUSTODY_ENCRYPTION_KEY` | Encrypts custody secrets at rest. Generate it with `openssl rand -base64 32`. |
| `NEXT_PUBLIC_CLERK_PUBLISHABLE_KEY` | Clerk publishable key for the dashboard. |
| `CLERK_SECRET_KEY` | Clerk secret key. |

The configurator also requires these. The stack starts without them, but most leave a core flow broken:

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| `CLERK_ISSUER` | Clerk issuer URL. Without it, dashboard sessions can't be verified, so sign-in fails. |
| `FRONTEND_URL` | The dashboard URL the browser loads. With `ENVIRONMENT=production`, the compose default, the API accepts only Clerk sessions issued to this origin, and won't start if it isn't an `http(s)` URL. |
| `SOLANA_RPC_DEFAULT_DEVNET_API_KEY_URL` | The devnet endpoint Sandbox projects read and send through. Without it, they get `503 RPC_UNAVAILABLE`. |
| `SIGNING_PROVIDER` | The configurator writes `local` unless you pick another provider. The API reads it only at startup, where `local` (also its value when unset) requires `SDP_DEPLOYMENT_MODE=self_hosted`. |
| `CUSTODY_PRIVATE_KEY` | With local signing selected: SDP offers the local signer only while this is set. |
| `CREDENTIAL_FINGERPRINT_PEPPER` | Without it, saving or rotating provider credentials in the dashboard fails. Keep it stable. |

`SOLANA_RPC_DEFAULT_MAINNET_API_KEY_URL` is optional: without it, SDP refuses Production projects' chain reads and sends.

The configurator generates `API_KEY_PEPPER`, `CREDENTIAL_FINGERPRINT_PEPPER`, and `CUSTODY_ENCRYPTION_KEY` for you, and can generate `POSTGRES_PASSWORD`.

## Database

The configurator's database choice (`DATABASE_MODE`) shapes the file, but isn't written to it.

- **Bundled:** set `POSTGRES_DB`, `POSTGRES_USER`, and `POSTGRES_PASSWORD`. The API and `sdp-migrate` build their connection string from them.
- **External:** set `DATABASE_URL` to your `postgresql://…` string, and the API and migrations connect there. The bundled `postgres` container still starts, unused, so it still needs `POSTGRES_PASSWORD`. The configurator hides that field and generates a value for it.

## Cache

The cache choice (`CACHE_MODE`) isn't written to the file either. For an external cache, set `REDIS_URL` to your `redis://…` or `rediss://…` endpoint. The bundled `redis` container still starts, unused.

## Signing providers

The configurator offers `local`, `fireblocks`, `privy`, `coinbase_cdp`, `para`, `turnkey`, and `utila`. Its list of providers to enable (`SIGNING_PROVIDERS`) only decides which credential fields it shows, and isn't written to the file. Each provider other than `local` needs its own credentials, such as an API key and secret for Fireblocks. Each project picks its signer when you set up custody in the dashboard.

Privy, Coinbase CDP, Para, and Turnkey are open to every organization. The others, `local` included, also need a per-organization activation: [First devnet deployment](/docs/self-hosting/first-devnet-deployment) shows how for the local signer.

For provider co-signers that run outside the stack, see [External co-signers](/docs/self-hosting/external-co-signers).

## Fee payment

SDP pays transaction fees through a Kora on each project's cluster, and the stack doesn't bundle one. The configurator's choice of clusters (`FEE_SPONSOR_CLUSTERS`) isn't written to the file: it shows each chosen cluster's fields. Without a Kora, sends SDP sponsors, such as payment transfers, answer `503 PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE`.

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| `KORA_DEVNET_URL` | The Kora that pays fees for Sandbox projects. |
| `KORA_DEVNET_RPC_URL` | The Solana RPC endpoint that Kora reads. SDP prices and settles sponsored fees through it. Set it with `KORA_DEVNET_URL`: the API won't start with only one of the two. |
| `KORA_DEVNET_API_KEY` | Optional. The API key your Kora requires, if any. |
| `KORA_DEVNET_CLOUD_RUN_AUDIENCE` | Optional. For a private Kora on Cloud Run: SDP sends it a Google identity token for this audience, which needs the API on Google Cloud and the Kora URL on the audience's `https` origin. |

The `KORA_MAINNET_*` variables do the same for Production projects.

## Advanced

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `SDP_IMAGE_REGISTRY` | `ghcr.io/solana-foundation/sdp` | Registry the images come from. |
| `SDP_VERSION` | `latest` | Image tag for every SDP service. Pin it to a release tag, such as `vX.Y.Z`, in production. |
| `SDP_API_PORT` | `8787` | Host port for the API. |
| `SDP_WEB_PORT` | `3000` | Host port for the dashboard. |
| `SDP_DOCS_PORT` | `3001` | Host port for these docs. |
| `TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS` | `false` | How to read `X-Forwarded-For`. `true` trusts the first address: use it only behind an ingress that replaces caller-supplied forwarding headers. `gclb` is for ingress restricted to a Google Cloud external Application Load Balancer, which appends the verified client address. With `false`, SDP can't see caller addresses: per-IP limits count every caller as one, and an IP allowlist refuses every request. |

`SDP_API_BASE_URL` (default `http://sdp-api:8787`) is how the dashboard's server reaches the API inside the Docker network. The browser-facing `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` URLs default to `localhost`, such as `http://localhost:8787` for the API and `http://localhost:3000` for the dashboard. Change them, and `FRONTEND_URL`, when you put the services behind your own domains.

`compose.yml` also reads `SDP_RELEASE_CHANNEL`, which the configurator doesn't set. It decides which modules and providers the API and dashboard run (`experimental`, `beta`, or `stable`), and defaults to `experimental`.

---

### Upgrade & Backup
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/self-hosting/upgrade-and-backup

> Move a self-hosted Solana Developer Platform to a new release and protect its data.

Upgrade to a new release, roll back, and back up the data that matters.

## Upgrade

A release ships new images and an updated `compose.yml`.

1. **Refresh the install files.** Re-run the install script. It replaces `compose.yml` with the new release's, verified against its checksums. It never touches `.env`, keeps an existing `.env.example`, and prints a link to the new release's template so you can check for new variables.

   ```bash title="Terminal"
   curl -fsSL https://github.com/solana-foundation/solana-developer-platform/releases/latest/download/install.sh | bash
   ```

   To install a specific release instead of the latest, set `INSTALL_VERSION` to its tag:

   ```bash title="Terminal"
   curl -fsSL https://github.com/solana-foundation/solana-developer-platform/releases/latest/download/install.sh | INSTALL_VERSION=vX.Y.Z bash
   ```

2. **Pin the version.** Set `SDP_VERSION` in `.env` to the same release tag, not `latest`, so every service runs one known build.

3. **Pull and restart.**

   ```bash title="Terminal"
   cd ~/sdp
   docker compose pull
   docker compose up -d
   ```

   `sdp-migrate` applies any new database migrations before the API starts.

4. **Verify** that the services are healthy, as in the [Quickstart](/docs/self-hosting/quickstart#4-verify).

### Roll back

To run the previous release again, re-run the install script with its tag in `INSTALL_VERSION`, set `SDP_VERSION` to that tag, and run `docker compose up -d`.

Migrations don't reverse. If the newer release applied any, restore a backup taken before the upgrade instead of only switching versions.

## Backup

Two things hold your state:

- **The Postgres database:** all platform data. The bundled database lives in the `sdp-postgres-data` volume (`sdp_sdp-postgres-data` in `docker volume ls`). Back up an external `DATABASE_URL` with your database provider's tools.
- **Your `.env`:** configuration and secrets you can't regenerate. Without the same `API_KEY_PEPPER`, no existing API key matches. Without the same `CUSTODY_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, SDP can't decrypt the custody secrets it stored, such as local wallet keys. Keep the file in a secret manager.

Redis is a cache and doesn't need a backup.

### Back up the database

Take a logical dump with `pg_dump` inside the running container. Running it through `sh -c` lets it read `POSTGRES_USER` and `POSTGRES_DB` there, so custom values work:

```bash title="Terminal"
cd ~/sdp
docker compose exec -T postgres \
  sh -c 'pg_dump -U "$POSTGRES_USER" "$POSTGRES_DB"' > sdp-backup.sql
```

Keep dumps off the host, on a schedule that fits your recovery needs.

### Restore the database

A plain `pg_dump` holds the full schema and the migration history, so restore it into an **empty** database and let the stack start on top. Restoring over an already migrated database collides with the schema `sdp-migrate` created.

```bash title="Terminal"
cd ~/sdp
docker compose down                       # stop every service
docker volume rm sdp_sdp-postgres-data    # discard the current database (destructive)
docker compose up -d postgres             # start a fresh, empty Postgres
until docker compose exec -T postgres \
  sh -c 'pg_isready -U "$POSTGRES_USER"' >/dev/null 2>&1; do sleep 1; done
docker compose exec -T postgres \
  sh -c 'psql -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB"' < sdp-backup.sql
docker compose up -d                      # start the rest
```

On that final `up`, `sdp-migrate` skips every migration the dump already records, so an older dump gets only the newer migrations.

Restore the matching `.env` too, so secrets such as `CUSTODY_ENCRYPTION_KEY` match the data they protect. Restore an external `DATABASE_URL` through your database provider instead of the bundled `postgres` service.

---

### Troubleshooting
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/self-hosting/troubleshooting

> Diagnose common startup and configuration failures on a self-hosted stack.

Most problems show up at startup. Start with the service state and the API logs:

```bash title="Terminal"
cd ~/sdp
docker compose ps
docker compose logs -f sdp-api
```

## Docker is not ready

The install script checks Docker first. If it reports that Docker isn't installed, that Compose v2 is unavailable, or that the daemon isn't reachable, install or start Docker and retry. See the [Docker Engine](https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/) and [Compose](https://docs.docker.com/compose/install/) install guides.

## A required variable is missing

`compose.yml` stops with a message such as `set POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env` when a required variable is unset. Make sure `.env` sits next to `compose.yml` and sets every required variable. The [configurator](/docs/self-hosting/configurator) writes a complete file, and the [environment reference](/docs/self-hosting/env-reference) lists what's required.

## Images won't pull

If `docker compose pull` reports access denied or a missing manifest:

- Check that `SDP_IMAGE_REGISTRY` and `SDP_VERSION` name a registry and tag you can reach. Release tags look like `vX.Y.Z`.
- Pull one image directly to see the underlying error, for example `docker pull ghcr.io/solana-foundation/sdp/sdp-api:latest`.
- If the registry is private, run `docker login` for it first.

## Port already in use

The API, dashboard, and docs use ports `8787`, `3000`, and `3001` by default. If another process holds one, that service can't bind. Set `SDP_API_PORT`, `SDP_WEB_PORT`, or `SDP_DOCS_PORT` in `.env`, update the browser-facing URLs that name that port (the `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` URLs, and `FRONTEND_URL` for the dashboard), and run `docker compose up -d` again.

## Migrations failed

`sdp-migrate` runs before the API starts. If it fails, the API stays down. Read its logs:

```bash title="Terminal"
docker compose logs sdp-migrate
```

A failure here is usually a database connection problem. Check `POSTGRES_*` (or `DATABASE_URL`), and that `postgres` shows as healthy in `docker compose ps`.

## Database connection refused

The API and migrations wait for Postgres to report healthy before they start. If they still can't connect, check the credentials in `.env`. With an external database (`DATABASE_URL` set), check that it's reachable from inside the Docker network.

## Dashboard sign-in fails

Most sign-in failures are Clerk configuration. Check `NEXT_PUBLIC_CLERK_PUBLISHABLE_KEY`, `CLERK_SECRET_KEY`, and `CLERK_ISSUER` against your Clerk application, and that the keys belong to the instance (development or production) you mean to use. Then look for these messages:

- `Clerk token missing organization` or `Clerk token has no usable email claim`, in the failing request's `401` response: the session token lacks the claims in the [Clerk setup guide](https://github.com/solana-foundation/solana-developer-platform/blob/main/apps/sdp-api/docs/self-hosting/clerk-setup.md).
- `Clerk session refused: not issued to the dashboard`, in the API logs: `FRONTEND_URL` isn't the origin the dashboard loads from. With `ENVIRONMENT=production`, the API accepts only sessions issued to that origin.

## The local signer isn't offered

If the local provider is missing from the dashboard, `CUSTODY_PRIVATE_KEY` isn't set. If choosing it returns `Local requires manual activation for this organization.`, add the organization override from [First devnet deployment](/docs/self-hosting/first-devnet-deployment), and check that the Clerk webhook reaches the API.

## Still stuck?

Collect the failing service's logs and your `.env` settings with the secrets removed, then open an issue on the [project repository](https://github.com/solana-foundation/solana-developer-platform).

---

### External Co-Signers
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/self-hosting/external-co-signers

> Host provider-specific signing services outside the default self-hosted SDP stack.

Some signing providers need a co-signer or automation process that you run beside the SDP API. Run it outside `compose.yml`, which starts only SDP's own services: a co-signer has its own secrets, identity, ingress, and availability needs.

## Production pattern

Run each co-signer on a managed container service, such as Google Cloud Run or your cloud's equivalent.

- Use the image and runtime the provider or your operator team supplies.
- Store co-signer secrets in a cloud secret manager, never in the SDP `.env`.
- Give the co-signer a dedicated service account that can read only the secrets it needs.
- Set ingress and invoker IAM for the provider's flow. Keep ingress private or authenticated unless the provider needs a public callback.
- Keep at least one instance running (`minScale: 1` on Cloud Run) when callback latency or availability matters. Scale to zero only when cold starts are acceptable.
- Separate development, staging, and production co-signers by provider account, cloud project, service account, and secrets.
- Alert on failed signing attempts, container restarts, authentication failures, and stale or expired key material.

## Utila

SDP signs with Utila directly: select `utila` in the configurator and fill in its `UTILA_*` credentials. SDP submits each transaction to Utila and polls until it's signed, up to `UTILA_MAX_POLL_ATTEMPTS` times every `UTILA_POLL_INTERVAL_MS` (60 tries, a second apart, by default). Like the local signer, Utila needs a per-organization activation.

`UTILA_DESIGNATED_SIGNERS` lists the Utila users asked to sign each transaction. Left empty, it's the service account itself.

If your Utila setup runs an automated co-signer, host it outside the stack. `infra/utila/cloud-run/` in the repository has Cloud Run scaffolding for one: a service template and a deploy script for an image you supply.

---

## Reference

### Overview
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/reference

> The API reference and its conventions, AI resources, the Postman collection, and provider onboarding.

Reference material for building on SDP:

- [API reference](/docs/reference/api): every public endpoint, by family.
- [API conventions](/docs/reference/conventions): errors, pagination, rate limits, and versioning.
- [AI resources](/docs/reference/docs-for-ai): machine-readable docs for coding agents.
- [Postman collection](/docs/reference/postman-collection): the public API, ready to import.
- [Provider onboarding](/docs/reference/provider-onboarding): add your infrastructure integration to SDP.

---

### Infrastructure Provider Onboarding
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/reference/provider-onboarding

> Add an infrastructure provider integration to SDP through the self-service contribution process.

SDP accepts infrastructure provider integrations in the categories below. An onboarded provider is listed as an available integration, not an endorsed or recommended partner. Institutions using SDP are responsible for their own provider due diligence.

## Start here

Pick your category, complete its intake form, and review its criteria before you open a pull request.

| Category | Intake form | Criteria |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Custodial enterprise wallet | [Complete custody intake](https://solanafoundation.typeform.com/to/wShiq9SN) | [Download custody criteria PDF](/provider-onboarding/custodial-wallet-vendor.pdf) |
| RPC infrastructure | [Complete RPC intake](https://solanafoundation.typeform.com/to/cq5m65jI) | [Download RPC criteria PDF](/provider-onboarding/rpc-providers.pdf) |

A module's own categories publish their intake on that module's pages. If your category has no published intake, contact the SDP team before you open a pull request.

## Onboarding steps

1. Review the criteria PDF for your category.
2. Complete the matching intake form.
3. Provide sandbox or playground API access.
4. Share documentation, test credentials, supported networks, rate limits, and sandbox limitations.
5. Build the SDP integration, with tests and docs.
6. Open a pull request that links to the intake submission or tracking issue.

The SDP team reviews intake completeness within five business days. Gate evaluation usually takes one to three weeks, depending on the category, how complete the documentation is, and the technical validation it needs.

## Evaluation

Each category uses the criteria linked above. A review starts with hard gates, then a scored evaluation where the category has one. SDP evaluates:

- Solana compatibility for the category.
- Stable sandbox or playground access.
- Clear API and integration documentation.
- Predictable error handling and testability.
- Operational readiness and support.
- The regulatory, compliance, or security posture the category requires.

A provider that doesn't clear the required gates may be tracked for future support, but isn't presented as available until the gaps close. A provider that clears evaluation must still be configured by the deployment. It's then either generally available to every organization, or needs a per-organization Manual Provider Activation while commercial or operational onboarding finishes.

## Access requirements

Provide access that supports repeatable validation:

- Sandbox API keys or equivalent credentials.
- Test accounts, wallets, endpoints, or settlement rails, when the category needs them.
- The Solana networks you support.
- Known rate limits, feature flags, and sandbox limitations.
- A technical support contact for the review.

## Pull request expectations

An SDP infrastructure provider contribution usually includes:

- Provider metadata and capability registration.
- API support for setup, configuration, and the category's runtime operations.
- Dashboard support, where it applies.
- Tests for setup, success paths, failure states, disabled configuration, and missing credentials.
- User-facing docs for setup, sandbox behavior, and provider limits.

Open the pull request once intake is complete, or once the SDP team has opened a tracking issue while intake is finalized.

---

### Postman Collection
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/reference/postman-collection

> Download the public SDP API as a Postman collection, generated from the OpenAPI contract.

The collection is generated from the same public OpenAPI contract as the [API reference](/docs/reference/api), and holds every family published there. Internal families, such as `admin`, `onboarding`, `organizations`, `members`, and `api-keys`, are left out.

<a href="/docs/postman/collection.json" download>Download Postman collection</a>
  <a href="/docs/postman/collection.json">Open raw JSON</a>

After you import it, set two collection variables:

- `baseUrl`: the API host to call. It defaults to `https://api.solana.com`.
- `sdpApiKey`: your API key (`sf_...`), sent as a bearer token.

## Idempotency keys

Each route that requires an `Idempotency-Key` sends the one saved in its `idempotencyKey.<operationId>` collection variable. Postman creates the key when the variable is empty. It clears the key only after a final `2xx`, a replayed refusal, or a `422` other than `IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED`.

Every other answer keeps the key for the next send. That covers a transfer, batch, or schedule still `pending` or `processing` (poll it with `GET` until it's final), a timeout, a `5xx`, a `409` or `429`, a `400`, `401`, or `403` refusal, and `422 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED`. See [Idempotency](/docs/developing-with-sdp/idempotency#the-dashboard-and-the-postman-collection).

---

## Conventions

### API conventions
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/reference/conventions

> What every SDP API call has in common, from how it authenticates to how it fails.

Every route follows these rules:

- [Authentication](/docs/developing-with-sdp/authentication): send an API key in the `Authorization` header. Its grants decide what it can do.
- [Environments](/docs/developing-with-sdp#environments): a project runs in sandbox (devnet) or production (mainnet-beta), and its keys work in that environment only.
- [Idempotency](/docs/developing-with-sdp/idempotency): send an `Idempotency-Key` to retry a mutation safely. Routes that move money require one.
- [Errors](/docs/reference/conventions/errors): one error envelope, with a code to branch on.
- [Pagination](/docs/reference/conventions/pagination): lists return one page at a time.
- [Rate limits](/docs/reference/conventions/rate-limits): each API key gets a set number of requests per minute.
- [Versioning](/docs/reference/conventions/versioning): the version is in the path, and a breaking change gets a new one.

A successful JSON response wraps its payload in `data`, with `meta.requestId` beside it. A `204` has no body, and the health checks answer with their own. Every response also carries the request ID in `X-Request-ID`: quote it when you report a problem.

---

### Errors
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/reference/conventions/errors

> A failed request returns an HTTP error status and one error envelope, with a code to branch on.

A failed request returns an error status and this body. The health checks are the exception: each answers with its own body, as its page shows.

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "FORBIDDEN",
    "message": "Access denied"
  },
  "meta": { "requestId": "req_..." }
}
```

- `code` is stable: branch on it, not on `message`, which is for people and can change.
- `details`, when present, says more, such as which field failed validation.
- `meta.requestId` identifies the request. Quote it when you report a problem.

## Statuses

| Status | Means | Common codes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `400` | The request is malformed or fails validation. | `BAD_REQUEST`, `IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REQUIRED` |
| `401` | The API key is missing, invalid, expired, or revoked. | `UNAUTHORIZED`, `INVALID_API_KEY`, `EXPIRED_API_KEY`, `REVOKED_API_KEY` |
| `403` | The key lacks the grant or wallet access the request needs, or the call comes from an IP address the key or its organization doesn't allow (`details.reason` is `ip_not_allowed`). | `FORBIDDEN`, `INSUFFICIENT_PERMISSIONS` |
| `404` | Nothing with that ID exists in the project. | `NOT_FOUND` |
| `409` | The request conflicts with the resource's state, or an earlier request with the same idempotency key is still running or never recorded its outcome. | `CONFLICT`, `IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_IN_FLIGHT`, `IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_OUTCOME_UNKNOWN` |
| `413` | The request body is larger than 1 MB. | `PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE` |
| `422` | The request is well formed but can't go ahead: its idempotency key was used for a different request, the transaction fee sponsor rejected the transaction, or the wallet's policy at its custody provider refused to sign it. | `IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED`, `SIGNING_REJECTED`, `CUSTODY_POLICY_REFUSED` |
| `429` | Too many requests. See [Rate limits](/docs/reference/conventions/rate-limits). | `RATE_LIMITED` |
| `500` | Something failed inside SDP. | `INTERNAL_ERROR` |
| `502` | Solana RPC or a provider answered, but with something SDP couldn't use, or the custody provider failed or timed out while signing. | `SOLANA_RPC_ERROR`, `PROVIDER_RESPONSE_INVALID`, `CUSTODY_ERROR` |
| `503` | SDP, or a provider it depends on, is unavailable for now, or a provider isn't configured for the project's environment. | `SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE`, `PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE`, `PROVIDER_NOT_CONFIGURED`, `RPC_UNAVAILABLE` |

Each operation's page lists its statuses and shows a success example. The OpenAPI spec carries every response schema.

## Retrying

- `400`, `401`, `403`, `404`, `413`, and `422`: fix the request before you send it again.
- `422 CUSTODY_POLICY_REFUSED`: the wallet's policy at its custody provider refused to sign. The message names the provider. Review the policy there, or change the request, before you send it again.
- `409 CONFLICT`: read the resource's current state, then decide.
- `409 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_IN_FLIGHT` and `429`: wait for `Retry-After`, then retry with the same `Idempotency-Key`.
- `409 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_OUTCOME_UNKNOWN`: final for that key. Read the resource with `GET` to see whether the request ran, then send it again with a new key.
- `503 RPC_UNAVAILABLE`: `details.reason` says why Solana RPC was unavailable. `upstream_unavailable` is temporary: wait for `Retry-After`, then retry as the `5xx` rule below says. `not_configured` and `cluster_mismatch` are SDP configuration problems that a retry won't fix. Quote `meta.requestId` when you report one.
- `503 PROVIDER_NOT_CONFIGURED`: a provider the request needs, such as the custody provider that signs for the wallet, isn't configured for the project's environment. A retry won't fix it until that changes. Check the provider's configuration, or quote `meta.requestId` when you report it.
- `5xx`: most routes store the error and return it again to a same-key retry. Read the resource with `GET` to see whether the request took effect, then retry with a new key. On the routes that move money, a same-key retry runs again and never acts twice.

[Idempotency](/docs/developing-with-sdp/idempotency) covers what each retry returns.

---

### Pagination
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/reference/conventions/pagination

> Lists return one page at a time, by page number on most routes and by cursor on a few.

Each list operation's page says which style it uses, with its default and largest page size.

## Page numbers

Most lists take `page` (from 1) and `pageSize`. The page's items are in `data`, and `meta` says where you are:

| Field | Means |
| --- | --- |
| `total` | Items across every page |
| `page` | This page's number |
| `pageSize` | Items per page |
| `hasMore` | Whether a later page exists |

Ask for the next `page` while `hasMore` is `true`.

## Cursors

A few lists take a `limit` and a cursor parameter instead. Each page returns a `nextCursor`: send it back in the cursor parameter the operation names, such as `cursor`, to get the next page. It's `null` on the last page.

---

### Rate limits
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/reference/conventions/rate-limits

> Each API key gets a set number of requests per minute, by its tier, and responses usually say how many are left.

Requests count against a limit per minute. Under `/v1`, a request with an API key counts against that key's tier (keys start on `standard`), and one without a key counts against its IP address. Outside `/v1`, every request counts against its IP address, even one that sends a key. The health checks and a few other public routes aren't limited.

| Caller | Requests per minute |
| --- | --- |
| An API key on the `standard` tier | 100 |
| An API key on the `elevated` tier | 500 |
| An API key on the `unlimited` tier | 10,000 |
| No API key, per IP address | 20 |

Some operations also have a tighter quota of their own, counted per key (or signed-in member) and per organization. They can return `429` before the key reaches its tier's limit. While SDP's counter store is unavailable, those operations refuse with `503` rather than run uncounted.

Responses usually say where you stand. The headers are left off while the counter store is unavailable, so don't depend on them:

| Header | Means |
| --- | --- |
| `X-RateLimit-Limit` | Requests allowed per window |
| `X-RateLimit-Remaining` | Requests left in this window |
| `X-RateLimit-Reset` | When this window ends, in Unix seconds |

Past a limit, a request gets `429` with the code `RATE_LIMITED` and a `Retry-After` header. Wait that many seconds before you send it again.

---

### Versioning
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/reference/conventions/versioning

> The API version is in every product route's path. /v1 is current, and a breaking change ships under a new major version.

Every product route's path starts with its version: `/v1` is the current contract. A breaking change ships under a new major version, such as `/v2`, never inside `/v1`. The health checks, `/health` and `/health/ready`, have no version.

The OpenAPI document's `info.version` counts revisions of that document for the current path version. It isn't the API's version.

## Notes
- Generated from docs source. Hidden or internal-only APIs are intentionally excluded.
